Cybersecurity advisories provide valuable guidance for defending against evolving threats, but their true value lies in how quickly organizations can translate recommendations into measurable security controls. With the release of the CISA Joint Cybersecurity Advisory AA26-194A, security teams now have concrete guidance to strengthen the security posture of their Internet-facing Cisco routers. It is crucial to acknowledge that actors sponsored by the Russian state are actively exploiting misconfigured and vulnerable networking devices, such as Cisco routers, to penetrate enterprise and critical infrastructure networks. In response, CISA, the NSA, and international partners have published AA26-194A, which provides clear guidance on hardening these devices against these threats.

It is important to start assessing your Cisco routers in accordance with the advisory’s recommendations.

Understanding CISA AA26-194A

CISA is committed to enhancing cybersecurity and regularly publishes periodically Joint Cybersecurity Advisories in collaboration with the National Security Agency (NSA) and other international partners. AA26-194A, titled Improve Router Hygiene to Protect Against Russian State-Sponsored Targeting, delivers crucial insights based on real-world threat intelligence, incident response findings, and observed attacker techniques.

This advisory shows that attackers exploit weak configurations, legacy management protocols, insecure administrative access, and unsupported devices to infiltrate enterprise networks. 

It is crucial to implement the advisory’s recommendations, which focus on fundamental security practices. These include using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), restricting management access, disabling unnecessary services, removing insecure default configurations, maintaining updated software versions, and continuously monitoring network device configurations. Taking these steps is essential for ensuring robust network security and resilience against potential threats.

The recommendations in AA26-194A help close this configuration gap by guiding organizations toward secure practices that strengthen the security posture of their Cisco network devices.

items.title: Binance’s $6.3bn heist: how one laptop opened the door to the biggest crypto theft in history
items.summary: Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume, has confirmed that attackers stole an estimated $6.3 billion (around £4.7 billion) in digital assets on Thursday evening, in what is now the largest cryptocurrency theft on record. The figure is roughly four times the $1.5 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025, the previous record-holder. According to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs, funds began leaving Binance wallets at around 20:05 UTC on 29 October, spread across ten blockchains including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron, the XRP Ledger and Solana. Most of the money was gone within roughly 20 minutes. Binance suspended deposits and withdrawals and, by late Thursday, said around $3 billion had been frozen with help from stablecoin issuers, partners, and law enforcement. Tether and Circle alone froze more than $2.5 billion in USDT and USDC. Binance’s preliminary findings point to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which the exchange says gave an attacker access to a service container that could submit withdrawals. The company says it has found “no evidence of any wallet private key leak” and has promised a detailed technical post-mortem once its investigation concludes. Co-CEO Yi He said the exchange would cover all hacking losses, drawing on its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and company funds. Markets reacted quickly. Bitcoin fell around 5% to below $77,000 in the hours that followed, while Binance’s own BNB token dropped about 8%. The vault held. The process didn’t. For security professionals, the size of the theft is only part of the story. What sets this incident apart is where the attackers chose to strike. “I’ve followed a lot of crypto thefts, and the Binance attack stands out less for the money than for how it was done,” said Jayant Dave, APAC CISO at Check Point . “The attackers didn’t break the encryption or steal the private keys. They took over the system that tells the keys what to sign.” Dave continued: “Binance’s early findings for now point to one compromised engineer’s laptop. From there, the attackers reached a service that could submit withdrawals, and billions moved within minutes. That’s the lesson: a strong vault doesn’t matter if someone controls the process that opens it.” TRM’s on-chain analysis supports that reading. On Ethereum, the attacker used EIP-7702 authorisations to make a Binance hot wallet execute a sweeper contract under their control, while the other nine chains saw ordinary signed transfers within the same window. TRM assesses that Binance’s hot wallet signing infrastructure was likely compromised, though the exchange has not yet published a root cause. “The Binance attack raises an important question about how organisations protect their most valuable assets,” said Simon Pamplin, CTO at Certes . “If attackers can move billions of dollars without obtaining the private keys themselves, we need to examine the systems and trusted processes that gave them the ability to authorise those transactions.” Samuel Hassine, CEO and co-founder at Filigran , agreed that the mundane nature of the entry point is what organisations should focus on. “The record figure will get the headlines, but the ordinary foothold is the lesson,” he said. “Binance says the attack may have started with a compromised engineer’s laptop, used to reach a service that submits withdrawals. It has since found further points of breach. By its own account, no wallet keys were stolen.” Entry point or root cause? Those further points of breach matter. Several experts cautioned against reducing a multi-billion-dollar compromise to a single infected device before the full investigation is complete. “A compromised laptop may explain where an attack started, but it does not, on its own, explain how billions of dollars could leave an exchange,” said Pieter Arntz, researcher at Malwarebytes . “The real question is what allowed that initial foothold to become access to withdrawal systems — and which safeguards failed to stop unauthorised transactions.” Arntz added: “Until the technical investigation is complete, blaming a single laptop risks confusing the entry point with the full cause of the breach.” Certes’ Pamplin made the same point. “Initial reports of a compromised engineer’s laptop are significant, but Binance has already indicated that the intrusion involved additional points of breach. The investigation will need to establish how that initial access developed into the ability to initiate withdrawals at this scale,” he said. “The distinction matters because compromising a system that can legitimately instruct transactions may be just as damaging as stealing the credentials or keys used to secure it.” For Pamplin, that is where long-held security assumptions start to break down. “This is where conventional security assumptions become dangerous. Organisations can have encryption, authentication and access controls in place, yet remain exposed if a compromised application or authorised process can operate within those controls. The real question is what an attacker can reach, read or instruct once that trusted environment is compromised.” “It reportedly only took one laptop” Whatever the full chain of events turns out to be, the image of a single endpoint leading to billions in losses has struck a nerve. “Billions of dollars have been stolen from Binance in a matter of minutes by hackers taking control of the process that authorises withdrawals. And it reportedly only took one laptop,” said Chris Dimitriadis, Chief Global Strategy Officer at ISACA . “It’s a stark reminder that you can spend a fortune protecting your most critical systems, but if just one device is compromised, then your security is only as strong as the weakest machine on the network.” Camellia Chan, CEO and co-founder of X-PHY , put it bluntly: “The biggest cryptocurrency heist in history may have started with a single compromised laptop. Such is the sophistication of hackers, that that’s all it can take.” She added that “Attackers are constantly looking for ways in, and for organisations handling sensitive financial information or critical infrastructure, employee laptops are particularly valuable targets.” “The reported cyberattack on Binance is staggering in both its scale and potential consequences,” said Jamie Akhtar, CEO and co-founder of CyberSmart . “The fact that cybercriminals were reportedly able to move billions in digital assets in a matter of minutes demonstrates just how devastating a successful attack can be.” For businesses, he said, “this is a powerful reminder that even the largest organisations with significant cybersecurity resources are not immune to attacks.” Jake Madders, co-founder and director of Hyve Managed Hosting , framed the incident as a question of access rather than defences. “The cyberattack affecting Binance highlights how attackers don’t always need to break through the front door. Sometimes, they simply exploit the people and systems already holding the keys,” he said. “Binance says initial checks suggest a compromised engineer’s laptop may have given attackers access to internal systems, enabling unauthorised withdrawals. This raises important questions about how access to critical systems is managed. Protecting where assets are stored is not enough if the routes into them are not equally secure.” The North Korea question TRM Labs has attributed the attack “with high confidence” to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking unit linked to the Lazarus Group. The firm points to small Tornado Cash withdrawals used to fund an operator wallet the day before the theft, along with staging and pre-obtained signatures that echo earlier DPRK-linked heists. Independent investigator ZachXBT has also named Lazarus as the likely attacker. “Blockchain analysts have linked the attack to TraderTraitor, the North Korean state-backed group behind the 2025 Bybit theft,” said Check Point’s Dave. “Governments haven’t confirmed that yet, but it fits a group that goes after people and processes, not cryptography.” Binance is not the only major exchange hit this autumn. In September, Bitget lost close to $388 million in a breach its chief executive also blamed on North Korea. “This attack isn’t a one-off either – five weeks ago, Bitget lost around USD 388 million the same way: keys untouched, control layer abused,” Dave said. “Two major exchanges in just over a month is a trend we cannot ignore.” Tim Rawlins, senior adviser and security director at NCC Group , said the targeting of a development engineer fits a well-established pattern. “This attack, reportedly on a development engineer, highlights that security is a critical element of every operational stage and personnel level. When security failures in trusted identities and administrative access can be targeted, attackers can exploit more than just the underlying technical vulnerabilities,” he said. “Given what we know about the activities of countries like North Korea in targeting cryptocurrency, it’s unsurprising that attackers are prepared to invest considerable effort in targeting individuals who have access to the building blocks of the exchanges.” Rawlins also flagged the role of artificial intelligence in accelerating these campaigns. “The increasing use of AI in attacks is supporting attackers to chain issues together in a way that might take them longer alone. Organisations are facing adversaries who are prepared to invest time and money to compromise their systems, if the return is large enough.” ISACA’s Dimitriadis echoed that view: “Hacker groups are often well resourced and patient, and they know how to target people. Organisations, particularly in financial services, that hold high-value assets must assume a breach will happen and plan for it ahead of time.” The stakes go beyond the exchange itself. TRM’s head of global policy, Ari Redbord, described the attack as “unprecedented”, warning that “When North Korea steals at this scale, the money funds weapons proliferation and other destabilising activity.” Not just a crypto problem It would be easy to treat the incident as a niche concern for crypto traders. Experts warn that would be a mistake. “For the public, the message is uncomfortable but important,” said Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress . “Your crypto holdings, your investment portfolio, and your pension fund’s exposure to digital assets can all be materially affected by a security failure at an institution.” Patel said the market reaction in the hours after the theft showed how far the consequences can travel. “When a cybersecurity incident sends shockwaves through crypto global markets, cybersecurity stops being a tech problem and starts being a systemic financial risk.” CyberSmart’s Akhtar agreed: “Beyond the financial losses, an incident of this magnitude raises serious concerns about the security of digital financial infrastructure and the potential consequences when highly sophisticated attackers gain access to critical systems.” For Check Point’s Dave, the same weakness exists well outside the crypto sector. “This goes well beyond crypto. Banks, payment providers, cloud platforms: any organisation whose automated systems move money or data on instruction carries the same risk,” he said. “Attackers have learned that the shortest route to the crown jewels often runs through one employee’s laptop and a trusted internal service.” Ordinary users also face knock-on risks. “This incident affects trust in cryptocurrency as a whole,” said Dimitriadis. “And high-profile incidents like this are often exploited by hackers on other platforms to trick users into taking immediate action that could compromise their crypto assets.” Spencer Starkey, Executive VP EMEA at SonicWall , noted that exchanges have long been in attackers’ sights. “Cryptocurrency exchanges are a popular target for cyberattacks, as they hold large amounts of valuable cryptocurrency. Cybercriminals will target cryptocurrency exchanges to steal cryptocurrency, disrupt operations, or even manipulate cryptocurrency prices,” he said. Starkey placed the Binance theft alongside a run of disruptive attacks closer to home. “Look at the last few weeks. Hackers pushed supermarket fridges across Europe to 50C, destroying food and starting fires. Criminals stole Legal Aid Agency records going back decades, including probation data. A GP dispensary couldn’t order medicines. Cybercriminals won’t wait for procurement to catch up.” Dimitriadis argued that responsibility for this kind of risk sits at the very top of an organisation. “This is ultimately a governance question, and it belongs in the boardroom, not just the security team. The fallout from an incident like this goes far beyond the money stolen – market confidence drops, customers move their assets elsewhere and regulators start asking questions.” Closing the gap So what should organisations that move money, or data, on instruction be doing now? The experts were broadly aligned: protect privileged people and devices, assume compromise, and make sure no single foothold can translate into unchecked authority. “So, protect the people with the most access first,” said Dave. “Treat developer and admin devices as high-value targets. Assume any machine or credential can be compromised and make sure none of them can move large sums without an independent check.” Speed and limits matter as much as prevention, he added. “Set hard limits on how much and how fast funds can move, and catch anomalies in seconds, not hours. Prevention has to come first, because once money spreads across multiple blockchains, getting it back is the exception.” NCC Group’s Rawlins stressed the basics. “As we have seen with many of the attacks against crypto exchanges and other platforms, good cyber hygiene and effective security fundamentals are key to defending against attacks that many organisations are still missing,” he said. “Securing trusted identities so funds can’t be moved unchallenged or other privileges exploited comes down to having phishing-resistant MFAs, just in time privileged access, tightly scoped and monitored human and non-human identities, and detection in place for anomalous activities.” Hyve’s Madders called for a stricter approach to access across the board. “The rule should be simple. People should only have access to the data and systems they need to do their jobs. This access should be tightly controlled, monitored, and removed as soon as it is no longer required. The same discipline must apply to external partners and third-party providers, whose access can create additional entry points for attackers.” “The Binance incident shows why access management needs to be treated as a fundamental part of cybersecurity, not an administrative afterthought,” he continued. “Ultimately, strong security depends on understanding who has access and what they can reach, not just protecting what is behind the door.” Certes’ Pamplin argued that controls need to sit closer to the transactions themselves. “Security needs to be enforced at the level of individual data flows and critical transactions, with cryptographic separation between systems and tightly controlled paths for sensitive operations. An attacker gaining access to one part of the environment should not automatically inherit the ability to move valuable assets across the rest of it.” Filigran’s Hassine urged organisations to map and test their own exposure. “Any company whose systems move money on instruction should know exactly which machines and accounts can trigger a transfer. Assume one of them will be compromised one day, and test whether the controls behind it hold.” CyberSmart’s Akhtar set out a similar checklist. “Protecting employee devices, implementing strong access controls and multi-factor authentication, and continuously monitoring for suspicious activity should be fundamental priorities. Organisations handling financial assets must also have additional safeguards in place, including strict transaction authorisation processes and controls that limit the damage a single compromised account or device can cause,” he said. “Employee cybersecurity awareness training is equally important, as attackers often exploit human vulnerabilities to gain their initial foothold.” X-PHY’s Chan agreed that training is necessary but not sufficient. “Businesses can train employees to recognise the warning signs of a cyberattack and if their devices are compromised, but cybersecurity capabilities must also be built into every layer of protection, starting with the hardware itself.” And for ISACA’s Dimitriadis, it comes back to leadership: “Good governance and building resilience mean the board treating cyber risk as a standing priority, investing in the right skills and making sure every employee is trained to recognise and resist targeted attacks.” Freezes, compensation and the road to recovery If there is a positive in the response so far, it is the speed with which a significant share of the stolen funds was frozen. “The estimated impact is around $6.3bn, four times the previous record. About $3bn was frozen within hours, with partners and law enforcement,” said Hassine. “That coordination is the part working well.” The rest is a different matter. TRM estimates the attacker still controls more than $2.4 billion in ether and bitcoin, and has already begun moving funds through decentralised exchanges and lending protocols including Uniswap, Aave and JustLend. “Credit to Binance for freezing funds quickly and committing to cover customer losses,” said Dave. “But the industry can’t keep relying on clean-up.” Binance’s pledge to make customers whole is significant, because crypto users have far less protection than bank customers if an exchange cannot or will not pay. “Unlike money held in a UK bank account, which may be protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) up to £120,000 per eligible depositor, cryptoassets generally do not benefit from any equivalent compensation regime,” said James Broomhall, Senior Associate at Grosvenor Law . “As a result, victims of major crypto thefts are often forced to pursue urgent tracing and recovery action through the courts, including Norwich Pharmacal applications to compel exchanges and other third parties to disclose information identifying fraudsters and tracing the movement of stolen assets.” What comes next Binance’s post-mortem should eventually show how a single endpoint became the ability to empty hot wallets across ten blockchains. Until then, much remains unknown. “As the investigation develops, we’ll gain a clearer understanding of how this attack unfolded,” said Chan. “But the key takeaway for businesses is already clear: security needs to be built into the very foundations of their systems, because there are no limits to the depths attackers will go to find a way in.” Pamplin agreed that organisations should not wait for the final report before acting. “The scale of this incident makes the consequences impossible to ignore. Security must be designed around the assumption that trusted systems can be compromised, with controls that prevent that compromise from becoming unrestricted authority over the assets they protect.” Or, as Hassine put it: “Record thefts start with ordinary footholds.” Dave’s warning may be the one that lingers longest: “The next attack will target the same weak point unless we close it first.”

Samuel Hassine, CEO and co-founder at Filigran, agreed that the mundane nature of the entry point is what organisations should focus on. “The record figure will get the headlines, but the ordinary foothold is the lesson,” he said. “Binance says the attack may have started with a compromised engineer’s laptop, used to reach a service that submits withdrawals. It has since found further points of breach. By its own account, no wallet keys were stolen.”

Entry point or root cause?

Those further points of breach matter. Several experts cautioned against reducing a multi-billion-dollar compromise to a single infected device before the full investigation is complete.

“A compromised laptop may explain where an attack started, but it does not, on its own, explain how billions of dollars could leave an exchange,” said Pieter Arntz, researcher at Malwarebytes. “The real question is what allowed that initial foothold to become access to withdrawal systems — and which safeguards failed to stop unauthorised transactions.”

Arntz added: “Until the technical investigation is complete, blaming a single laptop risks confusing the entry point with the full cause of the breach.”

Certes’ Pamplin made the same point. “Initial reports of a compromised engineer’s laptop are significant, but Binance has already indicated that the intrusion involved additional points of breach. The investigation will need to establish how that initial access developed into the ability to initiate withdrawals at this scale,” he said. “The distinction matters because compromising a system that can legitimately instruct transactions may be just as damaging as stealing the credentials or keys used to secure it.”

For Pamplin, that is where long-held security assumptions start to break down. “This is where conventional security assumptions become dangerous. Organisations can have encryption, authentication and access controls in place, yet remain exposed if a compromised application or authorised process can operate within those controls. The real question is what an attacker can reach, read or instruct once that trusted environment is compromised.”

“It reportedly only took one laptop”

Whatever the full chain of events turns out to be, the image of a single endpoint leading to billions in losses has struck a nerve.

“Billions of dollars have been stolen from Binance in a matter of minutes by hackers taking control of the process that authorises withdrawals. And it reportedly only took one laptop,” said Chris Dimitriadis, Chief Global Strategy Officer at ISACA. “It’s a stark reminder that you can spend a fortune protecting your most critical systems, but if just one device is compromised, then your security is only as strong as the weakest machine on the network.”

Camellia Chan, CEO and co-founder of X-PHY, put it bluntly: “The biggest cryptocurrency heist in history may have started with a single compromised laptop. Such is the sophistication of hackers, that that’s all it can take.” She added that “Attackers are constantly looking for ways in, and for organisations handling sensitive financial information or critical infrastructure, employee laptops are particularly valuable targets.”

“The reported cyberattack on Binance is staggering in both its scale and potential consequences,” said Jamie Akhtar, CEO and co-founder of CyberSmart. “The fact that cybercriminals were reportedly able to move billions in digital assets in a matter of minutes demonstrates just how devastating a successful attack can be.” For businesses, he said, “this is a powerful reminder that even the largest organisations with significant cybersecurity resources are not immune to attacks.”

Jake Madders, co-founder and director of Hyve Managed Hosting, framed the incident as a question of access rather than defences. “The cyberattack affecting Binance highlights how attackers don’t always need to break through the front door. Sometimes, they simply exploit the people and systems already holding the keys,” he said.

“Binance says initial checks suggest a compromised engineer’s laptop may have given attackers access to internal systems, enabling unauthorised withdrawals. This raises important questions about how access to critical systems is managed. Protecting where assets are stored is not enough if the routes into them are not equally secure.”

The North Korea question

TRM Labs has attributed the attack “with high confidence” to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking unit linked to the Lazarus Group. The firm points to small Tornado Cash withdrawals used to fund an operator wallet the day before the theft, along with staging and pre-obtained signatures that echo earlier DPRK-linked heists. Independent investigator ZachXBT has also named Lazarus as the likely attacker.

“Blockchain analysts have linked the attack to TraderTraitor, the North Korean state-backed group behind the 2025 Bybit theft,” said Check Point’s Dave. “Governments haven’t confirmed that yet, but it fits a group that goes after people and processes, not cryptography.”

Binance is not the only major exchange hit this autumn. In September, Bitget lost close to $388 million in a breach its chief executive also blamed on North Korea. “This attack isn’t a one-off either – five weeks ago, Bitget lost around USD 388 million the same way: keys untouched, control layer abused,” Dave said. “Two major exchanges in just over a month is a trend we cannot ignore.”

Tim Rawlins, senior adviser and security director at NCC Group, said the targeting of a development engineer fits a well-established pattern. “This attack, reportedly on a development engineer, highlights that security is a critical element of every operational stage and personnel level. When security failures in trusted identities and administrative access can be targeted, attackers can exploit more than just the underlying technical vulnerabilities,” he said.

“Given what we know about the activities of countries like North Korea in targeting cryptocurrency, it’s unsurprising that attackers are prepared to invest considerable effort in targeting individuals who have access to the building blocks of the exchanges.”

Rawlins also flagged the role of artificial intelligence in accelerating these campaigns. “The increasing use of AI in attacks is supporting attackers to chain issues together in a way that might take them longer alone. Organisations are facing adversaries who are prepared to invest time and money to compromise their systems, if the return is large enough.”

ISACA’s Dimitriadis echoed that view: “Hacker groups are often well resourced and patient, and they know how to target people. Organisations, particularly in financial services, that hold high-value assets must assume a breach will happen and plan for it ahead of time.”

The stakes go beyond the exchange itself. TRM’s head of global policy, Ari Redbord, described the attack as “unprecedented”, warning that “When North Korea steals at this scale, the money funds weapons proliferation and other destabilising activity.”

Not just a crypto problem

It would be easy to treat the incident as a niche concern for crypto traders. Experts warn that would be a mistake.

“For the public, the message is uncomfortable but important,” said Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress. “Your crypto holdings, your investment portfolio, and your pension fund’s exposure to digital assets can all be materially affected by a security failure at an institution.”

Patel said the market reaction in the hours after the theft showed how far the consequences can travel. “When a cybersecurity incident sends shockwaves through crypto global markets, cybersecurity stops being a tech problem and starts being a systemic financial risk.”

CyberSmart’s Akhtar agreed: “Beyond the financial losses, an incident of this magnitude raises serious concerns about the security of digital financial infrastructure and the potential consequences when highly sophisticated attackers gain access to critical systems.”

For Check Point’s Dave, the same weakness exists well outside the crypto sector. “This goes well beyond crypto. Banks, payment providers, cloud platforms: any organisation whose automated systems move money or data on instruction carries the same risk,” he said. “Attackers have learned that the shortest route to the crown jewels often runs through one employee’s laptop and a trusted internal service.”

Ordinary users also face knock-on risks. “This incident affects trust in cryptocurrency as a whole,” said Dimitriadis. “And high-profile incidents like this are often exploited by hackers on other platforms to trick users into taking immediate action that could compromise their crypto assets.”

Spencer Starkey, Executive VP EMEA at SonicWall, noted that exchanges have long been in attackers’ sights. “Cryptocurrency exchanges are a popular target for cyberattacks, as they hold large amounts of valuable cryptocurrency. Cybercriminals will target cryptocurrency exchanges to steal cryptocurrency, disrupt operations, or even manipulate cryptocurrency prices,” he said.

Starkey placed the Binance theft alongside a run of disruptive attacks closer to home. “Look at the last few weeks. Hackers pushed supermarket fridges across Europe to 50C, destroying food and starting fires. Criminals stole Legal Aid Agency records going back decades, including probation data. A GP dispensary couldn’t order medicines. Cybercriminals won’t wait for procurement to catch up.”

Dimitriadis argued that responsibility for this kind of risk sits at the very top of an organisation. “This is ultimately a governance question, and it belongs in the boardroom, not just the security team. The fallout from an incident like this goes far beyond the money stolen – market confidence drops, customers move their assets elsewhere and regulators start asking questions.”

Closing the gap

So what should organisations that move money, or data, on instruction be doing now? The experts were broadly aligned: protect privileged people and devices, assume compromise, and make sure no single foothold can translate into unchecked authority.

“So, protect the people with the most access first,” said Dave. “Treat developer and admin devices as high-value targets. Assume any machine or credential can be compromised and make sure none of them can move large sums without an independent check.”

Speed and limits matter as much as prevention, he added. “Set hard limits on how much and how fast funds can move, and catch anomalies in seconds, not hours. Prevention has to come first, because once money spreads across multiple blockchains, getting it back is the exception.”

NCC Group’s Rawlins stressed the basics. “As we have seen with many of the attacks against crypto exchanges and other platforms, good cyber hygiene and effective security fundamentals are key to defending against attacks that many organisations are still missing,” he said. “Securing trusted identities so funds can’t be moved unchallenged or other privileges exploited comes down to having phishing-resistant MFAs, just in time privileged access, tightly scoped and monitored human and non-human identities, and detection in place for anomalous activities.”

Hyve’s Madders called for a stricter approach to access across the board. “The rule should be simple. People should only have access to the data and systems they need to do their jobs. This access should be tightly controlled, monitored, and removed as soon as it is no longer required. The same discipline must apply to external partners and third-party providers, whose access can create additional entry points for attackers.”

“The Binance incident shows why access management needs to be treated as a fundamental part of cybersecurity, not an administrative afterthought,” he continued. “Ultimately, strong security depends on understanding who has access and what they can reach, not just protecting what is behind the door.”

Certes’ Pamplin argued that controls need to sit closer to the transactions themselves. “Security needs to be enforced at the level of individual data flows and critical transactions, with cryptographic separation between systems and tightly controlled paths for sensitive operations. An attacker gaining access to one part of the environment should not automatically inherit the ability to move valuable assets across the rest of it.”

Filigran’s Hassine urged organisations to map and test their own exposure. “Any company whose systems move money on instruction should know exactly which machines and accounts can trigger a transfer. Assume one of them will be compromised one day, and test whether the controls behind it hold.”

CyberSmart’s Akhtar set out a similar checklist. “Protecting employee devices, implementing strong access controls and multi-factor authentication, and continuously monitoring for suspicious activity should be fundamental priorities. Organisations handling financial assets must also have additional safeguards in place, including strict transaction authorisation processes and controls that limit the damage a single compromised account or device can cause,” he said. “Employee cybersecurity awareness training is equally important, as attackers often exploit human vulnerabilities to gain their initial foothold.”

X-PHY’s Chan agreed that training is necessary but not sufficient. “Businesses can train employees to recognise the warning signs of a cyberattack and if their devices are compromised, but cybersecurity capabilities must also be built into every layer of protection, starting with the hardware itself.”

And for ISACA’s Dimitriadis, it comes back to leadership: “Good governance and building resilience mean the board treating cyber risk as a standing priority, investing in the right skills and making sure every employee is trained to recognise and resist targeted attacks.”

Freezes, compensation and the road to recovery

If there is a positive in the response so far, it is the speed with which a significant share of the stolen funds was frozen. “The estimated impact is around $6.3bn, four times the previous record. About $3bn was frozen within hours, with partners and law enforcement,” said Hassine. “That coordination is the part working well.”

The rest is a different matter. TRM estimates the attacker still controls more than $2.4 billion in ether and bitcoin, and has already begun moving funds through decentralised exchanges and lending protocols including Uniswap, Aave and JustLend.

“Credit to Binance for freezing funds quickly and committing to cover customer losses,” said Dave. “But the industry can’t keep relying on clean-up.”

Binance’s pledge to make customers whole is significant, because crypto users have far less protection than bank customers if an exchange cannot or will not pay. “Unlike money held in a UK bank account, which may be protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) up to £120,000 per eligible depositor, cryptoassets generally do not benefit from any equivalent compensation regime,” said James Broomhall, Senior Associate at Grosvenor Law.

“As a result, victims of major crypto thefts are often forced to pursue urgent tracing and recovery action through the courts, including Norwich Pharmacal applications to compel exchanges and other third parties to disclose information identifying fraudsters and tracing the movement of stolen assets.”

What comes next

Binance’s post-mortem should eventually show how a single endpoint became the ability to empty hot wallets across ten blockchains. Until then, much remains unknown.

“As the investigation develops, we’ll gain a clearer understanding of how this attack unfolded,” said Chan. “But the key takeaway for businesses is already clear: security needs to be built into the very foundations of their systems, because there are no limits to the depths attackers will go to find a way in.”

Pamplin agreed that organisations should not wait for the final report before acting. “The scale of this incident makes the consequences impossible to ignore. Security must be designed around the assumption that trusted systems can be compromised, with controls that prevent that compromise from becoming unrestricted authority over the assets they protect.”

Or, as Hassine put it: “Record thefts start with ordinary footholds.”

Dave’s warning may be the one that lingers longest: “The next attack will target the same weak point unless we close it first.”

items.title: Cloudflare services for private origins is now generally available
items.summary: Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection . Your origin stays private, while web application firewall ( WAF ), caching , bot management , and Workers work just as they do for public origins. In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin. Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers. What is generally available today During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group. Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins: WAF and managed rules Bot management Rate limiting Caching Transform and rewrite rules Workers Some limitations remain. Argo Smart Routing and Aegis aren’t supported, and origin health checks require Load Balancing . See the developer documentation for the full list of current limitations. Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh , there’s no connector software to run on the origin either. How it works Create a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges, Use private network routing is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually. The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network. The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error. What the API looks like For customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record. POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records { "type": "A", "name": "app.example.com", "content": "10.0.0.50", "ttl": 300, "proxied": true, "private_routing": true } Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for app.example.com by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path: { "zone_name": "example.com", "ipv4_addresses": ["10.0.0.50"], "private_routing": true } The private_routing flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's IPsec , GRE , Cloudflare Tunnel , CNI , or Cloudflare Mesh. The beta post covers the routing layer in more detail. Get started Before you begin, you’ll need: The Private Origins entitlement on your account. Ask your account team to turn it on. Cloudflare One connectivity using IPsec, GRE, CNI, Cloudflare Tunnel, or Cloudflare Mesh . Unified Routing enabled on your account. New and existing accounts can upgrade through their account team. If you connect over Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh, you need Unified Routing enabled on your account and a return route for Cloudflare’s source ranges (100.64.0.0/12 for IPv4 and 2606:4700:cf1:5000::/64 for IPv6). New and existing accounts can upgrade to Unified Routing through their account team. Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that Use private network routing is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes. One note from the beta: if requests time out and nothing arrives at the origin, check the return route first. A missing route for Cloudflare’s source range was the most common setup failure we saw. Once enabled, follow our developer documentation , which walks through the full setup. What comes next Today’s release covers public traffic reaching private origins. Next, we’re working on private-to-private traffic: users, services, and AI agents on private networks reaching applications on other private networks through Cloudflare’s application services. Engineering work is underway, and we’re targeting a closed beta in early 2027. If you’d like to participate, talk to your account team. The goal is to give private applications the same protections and controls as public applications. An employee opening wiki.company.internal , for example, could benefit from WAF, rate limiting, and bot management. Service-to-service traffic between clouds and data centers could use those controls too, even when neither side touches the public Internet. For now, today’s release brings the WAF, caching, bot management, and Workers you use for public applications to private origins over connectivity you already operate. Questions or feedback? Join the conversation in our community forums or reach out to your account team.

Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection. Your origin stays private, while web application firewall (WAF), caching, bot management, and Workers work just as they do for public origins.

In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin.

Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers.

What is generally available today

During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group.

Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins:

  • WAF and managed rules
  • Bot management
  • Rate limiting
  • Caching
  • Transform and rewrite rules
  • Workers

Some limitations remain. Argo Smart Routing and Aegis aren’t supported, and origin health checks require Load Balancing. See the developer documentation for the full list of current limitations.

Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh, there’s no connector software to run on the origin either.

How it works

Create a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges, Use private network routing is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually.

The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network.

The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error.

What the API looks like

For customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record.

POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records
{
 "type": "A",
 "name": "app.example.com",
 "content": "10.0.0.50",
 "ttl": 300,
 "proxied": true,
 "private_routing": true
}

Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for app.example.com by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path:

{
 "zone_name": "example.com",
 "ipv4_addresses": ["10.0.0.50"],
 "private_routing": true
}

The private_routing flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's IPsec, GRE, Cloudflare Tunnel, CNI, or Cloudflare Mesh.

The beta post covers the routing layer in more detail.

Get started

Before you begin, you’ll need:

  1. The Private Origins entitlement on your account. Ask your account team to turn it on.
  2. Cloudflare One connectivity using IPsec, GRE, CNI, Cloudflare Tunnel, or Cloudflare Mesh.
  3. Unified Routing enabled on your account. New and existing accounts can upgrade through their account team.
  4. If you connect over Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh, you need Unified Routing enabled on your account and a return route for Cloudflare’s source ranges (100.64.0.0/12 for IPv4 and 2606:4700:cf1:5000::/64 for IPv6). New and existing accounts can upgrade to Unified Routing through their account team.

Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that Use private network routing is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes.

One note from the beta: if requests time out and nothing arrives at the origin, check the return route first. A missing route for Cloudflare’s source range was the most common setup failure we saw.

Once enabled, follow our developer documentation, which walks through the full setup.

What comes next

Today’s release covers public traffic reaching private origins. Next, we’re working on private-to-private traffic: users, services, and AI agents on private networks reaching applications on other private networks through Cloudflare’s application services.

Engineering work is underway, and we’re targeting a closed beta in early 2027. If you’d like to participate, talk to your account team.

The goal is to give private applications the same protections and controls as public applications. An employee opening wiki.company.internal, for example, could benefit from WAF, rate limiting, and bot management. Service-to-service traffic between clouds and data centers could use those controls too, even when neither side touches the public Internet.

For now, today’s release brings the WAF, caching, bot management, and Workers you use for public applications to private origins over connectivity you already operate.

Questions or feedback? Join the conversation in our community forums or reach out to your account team.

items.title: “A Ring Tone That I Cannot Hear” – Twenty Years Later
items.summary: My first post for this blog was in June 2006, 20 years ago: A Ring Tone That I Cannot Hear . Back then, I tested my hearing with Audacity, and I could hear a tone up to 14 kHz. 20 years later, I do the test again, and I can hear a tone up to 8 kHz. It’s no surprise that my hearing declined over the years, that happens to everybody. What did surprise me, or better said, what impressed me, is that a free and open-source tool like Audacity still exists after 20 years, and that I can just issue the exact same commands as 20 years ago!

items.title: Hackers Exploit Passwordless Telnet to Infect Linux Devices With New Kairos DDoS Botnet
items.summary: A new botnet called Kairos is spreading to Linux devices through a very old mistake: a Telnet service that accepts the root user with no password. Once inside, the attackers install a small Go-based program that turns the device into a node for DDoS operations. The campaign shows that basic security gaps still give attackers an easy path in. Kairos does not use a complex exploit or a zero-day flaw. The attackers connect to exposed Telnet services and log in as root with an empty password. Weak remote access has fueled many botnets before, including a VOIP-based botnet attacking routers that also relied on default Telnet logins. Analysts at Nozomi Networks identified the malware after their honeypots recorded three different IP addresses delivering Kairos samples. The Nozomi Networks Labs report describes it as a previously undocumented DDoS bot for Linux. The three samples were the same program. They differed only in the hard-coded command-and-control (C2) address and the Go compiler patch level, versions 1.27.0 and 1.27.1. This suggests the operator recompiles one codebase for each C2 server. Hackers Exploit Passwordless Telnet Every observed infection began the same way. The attacker guessed the default Telnet login, user root with an empty password. The operator then ran a short set of shell commands. First, uname -m checked the device’s processor type, and the payload requested later, x86_64 , matched it. This hints that the operator keeps a separate build for each architecture. Next, the commands moved into the /tmp folder, removed leftovers from earlier attempts, and downloaded the malware. Dropper commands used to download and execute the x86_64 payload (Source – Nozomi Networks) The dropper tries several download methods in turn: wget, curl, BusyBox wget, and finally TFTP. Each downloaded copy gets full permissions with chmod 777 and runs in the background. The BusyBox and TFTP fallbacks keep the loader working on small embedded systems that lack common tools. In the sample chain, the server at 172[.]86[.]85[.]39 hosted the payload on TCP port 8080 and also served as the C2 on port 9999. Once running, the bot connects to its single hard-coded IP address and sends a plain-text beacon, REGISTER linux amd64 . It then sends a blank line every two seconds to keep the session alive. If the link drops, it tries again every five seconds with no limit. The C2 can send only three commands: hold , which starts a flood, !ka , which stops all attacks and pauses the bot, and !ku , which lets it accept attacks again. Similar Telnet-driven threats include the Tengu Mirai botnet that reboots IoT devices when someone tries to remove it. How Kairos Floods Targets and How to Defend Against It Kairos does not send huge amounts of traffic. Instead, it opens hundreds or thousands of real TCP connections to a victim and keeps them open. The bot starts 128 workers per CPU core, with a minimum of 256, so a 16-core device opens 2,048 connections per attack. Each worker finishes a normal handshake, then sends one space character every five seconds to hold the socket open. If the target refuses the connection, the worker retries every 100 milliseconds, which creates a fast “connect storm.” The victim’s service slowly runs out of room and stops accepting real users. The bot is simple and has weaknesses. It has no persistence, no self-spreading, no command execution, and no anti-analysis features. Kairos bot registers to C2 (Source – Nozomi Networks) It tries to hide by renaming itself [kworker/0:1] to look like a Linux kernel thread. However, tools like ps and the /proc folder still show the real name. Since the bot completes real handshakes, its source IP is also visible to the victim. This is unlike KATARU IoT malware strain , which adds privilege escalation and encrypted C2 traffic. Defenders should disable Telnet, replace default or empty passwords, and block outbound traffic to the known C2 addresses on ports 9999 and 8080. Since the C2 address changes with each build, Nozomi advises relying on code-based detection. Teams can add an IDS rule for the plain-text REGISTER linux beacon and deploy the published YARA rule. They should also alert on any “kernel worker” process holding many outbound connections. A new botnet called Kairos is spreading to Linux devices through a very old mistake: a Telnet service that accepts the root user with no password.

Once inside, the attackers install a small Go-based program that turns the device into a node for DDoS operations. The campaign shows that basic security gaps still give attackers an easy path in.

Kairos does not use a complex exploit or a zero-day flaw. The attackers connect to exposed Telnet services and log in as root with an empty password.

Weak remote access has fueled many botnets before, including a VOIP-based botnet attacking routers that also relied on default Telnet logins.

Analysts at Nozomi Networks identified the malware after their honeypots recorded three different IP addresses delivering Kairos samples.

The Nozomi Networks Labs report describes it as a previously undocumented DDoS bot for Linux. The three samples were the same program.

They differed only in the hard-coded command-and-control (C2) address and the Go compiler patch level, versions 1.27.0 and 1.27.1. This suggests the operator recompiles one codebase for each C2 server.

Hackers Exploit Passwordless Telnet

Every observed infection began the same way. The attacker guessed the default Telnet login, user root with an empty password. The operator then ran a short set of shell commands.

First, uname -m checked the device’s processor type, and the payload requested later, x86_64, matched it. This hints that the operator keeps a separate build for each architecture.

Next, the commands moved into the /tmp folder, removed leftovers from earlier attempts, and downloaded the malware.

Dropper commands used to download and execute the x86_64 payload (Source – Nozomi Networks)

The dropper tries several download methods in turn: wget, curl, BusyBox wget, and finally TFTP. Each downloaded copy gets full permissions with chmod 777 and runs in the background.

The BusyBox and TFTP fallbacks keep the loader working on small embedded systems that lack common tools. In the sample chain, the server at 172[.]86[.]85[.]39 hosted the payload on TCP port 8080 and also served as the C2 on port 9999.

Once running, the bot connects to its single hard-coded IP address and sends a plain-text beacon, REGISTER linux amd64 . It then sends a blank line every two seconds to keep the session alive.

If the link drops, it tries again every five seconds with no limit. The C2 can send only three commands: hold, which starts a flood, !ka, which stops all attacks and pauses the bot, and !ku, which lets it accept attacks again. Similar Telnet-driven threats include the Tengu Mirai botnet that reboots IoT devices when someone tries to remove it.

How Kairos Floods Targets and How to Defend Against It

Kairos does not send huge amounts of traffic. Instead, it opens hundreds or thousands of real TCP connections to a victim and keeps them open. The bot starts 128 workers per CPU core, with a minimum of 256, so a 16-core device opens 2,048 connections per attack.

Each worker finishes a normal handshake, then sends one space character every five seconds to hold the socket open. If the target refuses the connection, the worker retries every 100 milliseconds, which creates a fast “connect storm.”

The victim’s service slowly runs out of room and stops accepting real users. The bot is simple and has weaknesses. It has no persistence, no self-spreading, no command execution, and no anti-analysis features.

Kairos bot registers to C2 (Source – Nozomi Networks)

It tries to hide by renaming itself [kworker/0:1] to look like a Linux kernel thread. However, tools like ps and the /proc folder still show the real name.

Since the bot completes real handshakes, its source IP is also visible to the victim. This is unlike KATARU IoT malware strain, which adds privilege escalation and encrypted C2 traffic.

Defenders should disable Telnet, replace default or empty passwords, and block outbound traffic to the known C2 addresses on ports 9999 and 8080.

Since the C2 address changes with each build, Nozomi advises relying on code-based detection. Teams can add an IDS rule for the plain-text REGISTER linux beacon and deploy the published YARA rule.

They should also alert on any “kernel worker” process holding many outbound connections. Exposed services remain a common entry point, as seen when a cPanel authentication bypass flaw was used to drop Mirai malware.

items.title: Photo ID, bank checks, face scan? The UK’s age-check options
items.summary: As preparation for the UK’s planned social media ban, Ofcom has set out four ways social media platforms could check whether users are aged 16 or over. The government and Parliament will decide how the ban works in practice. Ofcom is the regulator for the communications services in the UK. The BBC reports that Ofcom identified four ways to check someone’s age that it considers “highly effective.” Here’s what those checks would involve: Photo ID matching : Comparing a live image of you with the photo on an identity document, such as your passport, and checking the age information on that document. Bank-based checks: Using age information your bank already holds about you, with your consent. Facial age estimation : Using technology to estimate your age from your face. Ofcom says this technology has improved recently. Digital ID services : Using a digital identity service to prove your age, rather than presenting a physical document. Let’s think through what those checks could mean. Challenges The challenge isn’t simply checking someone’s age. It’s doing so without turning everyday internet use into an identity check. Photo ID matching brings highly sensitive documents and facial images into the process, which raises questions about how that information is handled and protected. The risks aren’t hypothetical: as I reported last year , a breach at a third-party support provider for Discord exposed government ID images belonging to around 70,000 users. Banking-based checks can be more privacy-preserving if they return only confirmation that someone meets the age threshold, rather than exposing financial information. But the important questions are what information each party receives, what gets retained, and whether the check can be linked to someone’s activity. Facial age estimation can avoid uploading an identity document, but it still processes a sensitive image and makes an imperfect prediction. Ofcom acknowledges that some technologies can be wrong by a few years around age 16, so people near the threshold may face an additional verification check. I would expect these checks to stop some underage access but not eliminate it. Previous restrictions have been followed by workarounds, including increased VPN use , borrowed credentials, and migration to services outside the restrictions. The danger is treating a successful age gate as proof that children are now safe, when it might push them into less regulated spaces. The effectiveness depends on how the checks are implemented. A VPN may help someone avoid a check triggered by their apparent location; it won’t, by itself, bypass an identity or facial check that is still required. Similarly, Ofcom says matching a live image to an ID is intended to make it harder to borrow someone else’s document. We shouldn’t assume every workaround defeats every method. But Ofcom accepts that some motivated children will get through. The meaningful test is how much harm these measures prevent, weighed against the privacy risks and barriers they introduce— not whether every user has completed a check. My personal preference is double-blind verification: a provider confirms that you meet the age requirement without learning which service you’re accessing, while the service receives proof of age without learning your identity. Proving you’re old enough shouldn’t mean revealing who you are. Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once. items.title: Hackers Use Zero-Click Coruna and DarkSword Exploits to Steal Sensitive Data From iPhones
items.summary: Hackers are using two powerful iPhone exploit kits, Coruna and DarkSword, to break into phones and steal private data. The victim only has to open a web page. There is no app to install and no prompt to accept. The scale is larger than many people expected. Researchers found 608 domains delivering Coruna-family code. These sites choose an exploit chain based on the iOS version on the phone. iPhones on iOS 17.2.1 or older get the original Coruna kit. Newer iPhones on iOS 18 get a chain built from DarkSword. Earlier reporting on the Coruna and DarkSword kits already showed how outdated iPhones are at risk from a single website visit. Analysts at Zimperium’s zLabs team identified and documented this activity in a detailed technical report published on October 29, 2026. They recovered both the browser code and the native payloads. They also matched 93 of the domains to 21 tracking servers. Hackers Use Zero-Click Coruna and DarkSword Exploits The infection starts with a page that looks normal. Zimperium found dating sites built for users in Brazil, Nigeria, and Indonesia. It also found AI-companion chat sites, crypto promotions, and streaming pages. While the visitor sees the decoy, a hidden frame loads the exploit in the background. Some pages tell TikTok users to tap “Open in browser” so the link opens in Safari, which is the browser the exploit needs. Nothing looks wrong on screen, so advice like “watch for strange behavior” does not help here. AI-companion chat and legitimate casino content (Source – Zimperium) Next, a script checks the iOS version and picks the right path. The Coruna chain uses CVE-2022-48503, a WebAssembly flaw in Safari, to read and write browser memory. It then bypasses pointer authentication, an Apple protection that signs code addresses so tampering is caught. After it escapes the browser, the native modules read and write kernel memory and change code-signing settings. They talk to their servers over encrypted traffic with certificate checks turned off. They also delete crash logs and Safari website data to cover their tracks. The DarkSword chain works in steps. Browser code runs first. It then breaks out through the GPU process and moves into mediaplaybackd, a system media service. In Zimperium’s test on an iPhone running iOS 18.6.2, the phone contacted the command server 144 times and pulled seven extra modules. One module was built to read Telegram’s local storage. The phone then sent out its Apple Notes database and a list of 214 installed apps. The same kit has also appeared across DarkSword’s growing web infrastructure that operators replace within days, as DarkSword’s growing web infrastructure reporting from Censys showed. Supply Chain Delivery and Ways to Stay Safe Not every infection starts with a bad link. SafeDep found matching Coruna code inside the backdoored art-template npm package that many developers had pulled into their sites. Any site using the bad versions served the exploit to its own visitors, so no suspicious lure domain was needed. Domain blocklists miss this route completely. Zimperium also spotted a fake jquery.min.js file loaded from a look-alike Google domain on a comic site, which then started the Coruna chain. Who is behind it remains unclear. Coruna was first built by a nation-state actor for targeted work, but its leak spread the toolkit to many groups. Delivery and tracking in the recovered infrastructure (Source – Zimperium) Some recovered code has Chinese-language comments. Zimperium says that only describes how the code was written, not who deployed it, so it ties its conclusions to the code and infrastructure only. The best defense is patching, because every CVE in these chains is already fixed. Apple even pushed an expanded iOS 18.7.7 update to more devices to block DarkSword, so users should check Settings for the newest version offered for their phone. People at higher risk, such as journalists, activists, and executives, should turn on Lockdown Mode. Everyone should treat unexpected “Open in Safari” prompts as a stop sign. Security teams should require patched iOS builds on all devices, including personal ones used for work. Mobile threat defense tools can flag odd crashes, unexpected restarts, and disabled code signing. Teams should also keep diagnostic logs for high-risk users, because the malware deletes local traces. Site owners should audit third-party scripts and enforce a strict Content Security Policy. Binance says a security incident affected approximately $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency. Its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop as a possible entry point. The exchange says it has frozen around $3 billion with help from blockchain partners. It has promised to cover all losses using its emergency fund and company funds. Binance is reportedly the largest cryptocurrency exchange by daily trading volume. What happened? In an update on October 30, Binance said attackers may have used a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. The company said: “We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak.” This doesn’t mean that one employee could simply transfer billions of dollars. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told BleepingComputer the attacker did not simply use one engineer’s permissions. The incident involved a more complex process, rather than a single “one-click” action. Binance also said investigators had identified additional breach points. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group associated with previous cryptocurrency thefts. TRM Labs estimates that about $6.36 billion left Binance wallets across ten blockchains, with most of it moving within about 20 minutes. What should Binance users do? Binance says approximately $3 billion has been frozen on-chain, while blockchain analysts have reported somewhat different totals. For now, those figures should be treated as developing estimates rather than a final accounting of recovered funds or the exchange’s ultimate losses. Binance.com users ( Binance.US was not affected) should check their accounts, avoid follow-up scams, and respond quickly if they spot signs of a separate compromise. Go directly to official updates. Open the Binance app or navigate to its support site yourself. Avoid logging in through unexpected messages claiming that you must urgently verify your account or claim compensation. items.summary: A new malware framework called NIK C2 is turning the OpenAI API into a tool for cybercriminals. Its Windows implant can dump passwords, record every keystroke, take hidden control of a desktop, and send the stolen data to an AI model for analysis, all inside the same session. The tool is a Go-based, 64-bit Windows remote access program. It talks to its server over TLS-secured WebSockets on port 443. It also uses an HTTP backup channel that checks in about every 250 milliseconds. All traffic is locked with AES-256-GCM encryption, and the implant rotates between three server tiers so a single takedown does not cut it off. Researchers at Cisco Talos identified the malware and published their findings on October 29, 2026. Talos found a live server in the wild and said, with moderate confidence, that NIK C2 is a working framework and not a proof of concept. The samples point to at least three versions, which suggests a skilled team that keeps adding features. Abusing OpenAI is not new. The earlier OpenAI Assistants API backdoor called SesameOp used the service to hide its command traffic. NIK C2 goes a step further by using the model as a built-in analyst. Hackers Weaponize OpenAI API The AI feature runs through a command named ai_generate . The operator sends a prompt, an API key, and a model name. The implant builds a request and sends it to the OpenAI Chat Completions endpoint from the victim’s computer. It waits up to 60 seconds, reads the answer, and returns the text to the attacker’s panel along with token-usage counts. If no model is named, it defaults to gpt-4. The most worrying detail is the key fallback. If the attacker leaves out an API key, the implant reads the OPENAI_API_KEY variable on the victim’s machine. NIK C2 implant’s operational architecture (Source – Cisco Talos) OpenAI then bills the victim, and the logs show the victim’s key, so nothing points back to the attacker. Talos calls this a deliberate design choice. This kind of AI-enabled malware is getting more attention from defenders. Talos has also released the open-source CAIRN toolkit , which hunts for AI endpoints, prompt templates, and API-key patterns inside suspicious files. Because normal apps use the same AI services, blocking those domains alone is not practical. Credential Theft, Remote Control, and Screen-Locking Ransomware The implant supports more than 52 commands. For theft, it copies browser databases from Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, and Firefox. It also grabs saved Wi-Fi passwords, Discord tokens, and desktop crypto wallets such as Exodus, Electrum, and Bitcoin Core. It also targets wallet extensions such as MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet, and Phantom. Two search patterns hunt the whole disk for files with names like “seed,” “mnemonic,” “private,” or “secret.” A keylogger streams each keystroke live to the attacker. Hidden VNC gives full desktop control that the victim cannot see. The implant also offers proxy tunnels and RDP session control to move deeper into a network. To stay hidden, the implant renames itself to names like svchost.exe and csrss.exe and patches AMSI so PowerShell scripts are not scanned. It also skips the UAC prompt with a fodhelper trick. It marks itself as a critical process, so ending it in Task Manager triggers a Blue Screen of Death. The ransomware module is simple but fast. It backs up the Master Boot Record, writes an HTML lock screen with the attacker’s Bitcoin or USDT wallet details, and opens it through the Windows mshta.exe utility , a trusted tool that attackers often misuse. A registry Run key named “SystemLock” brings the screen back after every restart. It does not encrypt files, so it leaves little forensic evidence. A separate bootkit-prep feature checks UEFI, BIOS, and Secure Boot status. Online activists regularly use open-source intelligence (OSINT) to “doxx” people from very few clues, meaning that even a leak of basic identity information can put someone in danger. items.title: Pre-SIEM Detection for MSSPs
items.summary: tl;dr Prime Detect runs detection rules on your clients’ event streams before data reaches the SIEM. It applies Sigma rules to events in transit, tags each match with a severity and a MITRE ATT&CK technique, and links related matches into attack chains. In client testing, about 7% of telemetry was tagged. MSSPs use Prime Detect to give every client the same 20,000+ detections regardless of which SIEM that client runs, to send less data into SIEMs they pay to operate, and to keep each client’s data inside its own pipeline. It works alongside the SIEMs you already run. It does not replace them. Contact Sales Why MSSPs are moving detection ahead of the SIEM An MSSP’s detection coverage is usually set by whatever each client’s SIEM can hold. That creates three problems that grow with every client you add. Uneven coverage. Clients run different SIEMs with different rule limits. The same threat can be caught for one client and missed for another, depending on the platform underneath. Ingest cost. Where you operate the SIEM, every event ingested is a cost against your margin, whether it carries a threat signal or not. Engineering load. Your detection engineers spend their time porting and tuning the same rules across platforms instead of building the detections clients actually pay for. Prime Detect moves detection upstream. Rules run on events as they stream through the pipeline, before any SIEM ingests them. Coverage depends on the compute you assign, not on each client’s SIEM. You then decide, per client, what reaches the SIEM. What Prime Detect does Detection in the stream Applies Sigma rules to events in transit, before SIEM ingest Runs 20,000+ detection rules plus your own custom detections, with no fixed rule ceiling Tags every match with a severity and a MITRE ATT&CK technique Links related matches into attack chains, so analysts see a sequence of activity instead of isolated alerts Tagged telemetry you can route Tags about 7% of telemetry, based on client testing Sends tagged events to the SIEM and the rest to warm or cold storage, by your rules Produces structured, ATT&CK-labeled events that AI triage and SOAR tools can use directly Deployment and control Runs on Kafka and Kubernetes you or your clients operate Keeps data inside the pipeline, with no outbound connection required Deploys air-gapped or in the cloud Available open source or under an Enterprise license How it fits with the SIEMs you already run Prime Detect sits between the event pipeline and the SIEM. Nothing in the SIEM has to change, so it works across a mixed client base. MSSPs typically deploy it in one of two ways: Shared, multi-tenant: one Prime Detect deployment in your environment, with detections and routing set per tenant. Per client: a deployment inside the client’s own infrastructure, for clients with strict data residency or air-gap requirements. Rollout follows the same three steps either way: Forward everything to the SIEM as today, with Detect tags added to matched events. Add a SIEM index or dashboard that raises Detect-tagged events as high-priority alerts. Once tuned, route untagged events to warm or cold storage to cut ingest. What Prime Detect does not do It does not replace the SIEM for centralized logging, search, investigation, or retention. It does not decide whether an incident is significant or reportable. Your incident process makes that call. It does not make data transfer decisions for you. Where data goes, and under which agreement, stays with your firm and your clients. NIS2, DORA, HIPAA, and GDPR: where Prime Detect fits MSSPs carry their own obligations and inherit their clients’.
