items.title: Researchers Hacked Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop Embedded Browsers
items.summary: Security flaws in the embedded browsers of Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop could enable code execution, file theft, and address-bar spoofing on developer machines . The findings published on October 29 show how browser features built into AI assistants can break security boundaries when given extra access to their host apps. The researchers named the attack class EMBRACE, short for an embedded browser trusted like a real one. These are separate flaws sharing one design problem. Features meant to help assistants preview projects, read pages, and track tabs gave untrusted content powers it should not have. According to Forever report, Cursor exposed a window.cursorBrowser.send() bridge that allowed any loaded page to send content into the agent’s instruction box without a user gesture. Embedded Browser Flaws in Popular AI Coding Tools Exploited Attackers could abuse its element-selected channel to hide instructions inside HTML attributes. The visible item looked harmless, while the agent received command fragments and instructions to join them into an npm installation command. A single Enter keypress could approve execution. When Cursor’s sandbox blocked installation, the agent independently retried outside it, allowing the package’s preinstall script to launch Calculator. Proof of execution: the package’s `preinstall` launched Calculator from a cold start in an empty workspace (source: Forever security ) Success depended on the model and was not guaranteed. The finding adds another browser entry point to risks covered in earlier Cursor prompt injection research . GitHub Copilot’s browser preview accepted address updates supplied by the page itself. It checked the address format but did not confirm that the reported location matched the page actually loaded. Researchers made an attacker-controlled page display github.com/login in the preview’s address bar. The agent also received that false location, although the page remained on the attacker’s server. A fake login form could therefore appear beneath a trusted address and mislead both the user and the assistant. Claude Desktop and VS Code restricted file access on the main page but failed to apply the same checks inside web workers, which run scripts in the background. A malicious local preview could start a worker and read files outside its project folder. Codex needed no worker bypass. Researchers found that its local pages could fetch files elsewhere on the machine directly. On macOS, the team usedDS_Store metadata to discover filenames and expand the search across folders. Their test collected SSH keys, .env files, npm tokens, and private documents. The demonstration sent data to a local receiver. An attacker could instead use a remote server. Delivery required opening a malicious local page, potentially through a link generated by the assistant itself. These findings sit alongside earlier Claude sandbox escape coverage . Forever Security says Cursor patched its flaw on October 1. GitHub independently fixed the spoofing issue in Copilot 1.1.29 on October 13, after researchers confirmed it in version 1.1.27. At publication, Codex and VS Code remained unpatched. Microsoft rejected the report on Workspace Trust, while OpenAI did not respond. Anthropic accepted its issue after an initial rejection, but the report gives no clear patch status. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Palo Alto Confirms Active PHP2Shell Exploitation Targeting Exposed PAN-OS Management Interfaces
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that attackers are actively exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. In its October 29, 2026, update, Unit 42 said it independently verified attacker tools used to combine the PHP flaws with a Linux kernel vulnerability and gain root access. items.summary: Use a short Python script with the official client’s helpers.scan, or the _search API with a point in time (PIT) and search_after. For quick pulls of up to 10,000 rows, ES|QL with format=json works straight from Kibana’s Dev Tools. Kibana Discover can generate a report too, but not in a format LogTotal reads today. If your integration preserved it, event.original holds the raw log line. Elastic is one of the most common foundations for in-house security analytics, from Elastic Security to self-built stacks. Prime Core has 23,722 detection rules for Elastic, mapped to 671 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Authentication. Create an API key in Stack Management → API keys with read and view_index_metadata on the indices you need. Send it as Authorization: ApiKey . On Elastic Cloud, the Elasticsearch endpoint is on your deployment’s overview page. Know where the data lives. Elastic Agent integrations write to data streams named logs- - . Linux authentication logs from the System integration, for example, land in logs-system.auth-default. Check for event.original . Many integrations don’t keep the raw line by default; it’s a “preserve original event” option. If it’s missing, the parsed fields are what you have, and that’s fine for a JSON upload. Data tiers. Searches against cold or frozen tiers are slower. Keep windows tight when the data is old. The examples follow the current Elastic documentation, checked October 2026. Option 1: Python with helpers.scan (recommended) import json, os from elasticsearch import Elasticsearch, helpers es = Elasticsearch("https://my-deployment.es.example.com:443", api_key=os.environ["ES_API_KEY"]) query = {"query": {"range": {"@timestamp": { "gte": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "lt": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"}}}} with open("elastic_auth_1019.jsonl", "w") as out: for hit in helpers.scan(es, index="logs-system.auth-*", query=query, size=1000): out.write(json.dumps(hit["_source"]) + "\n") For raw lines, write hit[“_source”].get(“event”, {}).get(“original”, “”) instead of the whole document. Option 2: ES|QL for quick pulls In Kibana Dev Tools: POST /_query?format=json { "query": """ FROM logs-system.auth-* | WHERE @timestamp >= "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z" AND @timestamp < "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, source.ip, message | LIMIT 10000 """ } Two catches. ES|QL returns 1,000 rows unless you set LIMIT, and it tops out at 10,000. The JSON response also comes as columns plus values, not as records. To turn it into one object per line, save the query body as query.json and run it through jq: curl -sS -H "Authorization: ApiKey $ES_API_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ "https://my-deployment.es.example.com/_query?format=json" -d @query.json \ | jq -c '.columns as $c | .values[] | [$c, .] | transpose | map({(.[0].name): .[1]}) | add' > esql_1019.jsonl Option 3: Export logs from Kibana UI (Discover) For smaller investigations, Kibana Discover lets you find, filter, and export logs directly from the browser without writing scripts. Open Discover. Sign in to Kibana and navigate to Analytics → Discover , or select Discover from the main navigation. Select your data. Choose the data view containing the logs you need, such as logs-system.auth-*. Make sure it includes the relevant Elasticsearch indices or data streams. Set the time range. Use the time picker in the upper-right corner to select the investigation period. Narrow the window to avoid exporting unnecessary events. Filter the logs. Use the search bar and available filters to isolate relevant events. For example, enter event.category: authentication to focus on authentication activity. Select the fields. Add useful columns such as @timestamp, host.name, user.name, source.ip, and message. If available, include event.original to preserve the raw log content. Export the results. Open More → Export → Tab results as CSV (in some versions, Share → CSV Reports ). Generate the report and download the CSV file. If the export is not downloaded immediately, find it under Stack Management → Reporting . Alternative: Copy logs as JSON. For a small selection of events, select the relevant rows in Discover, open the Selected menu, and choose Copy documents as JSON . Paste the copied content into a text editor and save it as a .json file. Only the fields included in the current table selection may be copied. Limitations. CSV reports are intended for moderate-sized exports and have row-count and file-size limits that depend on the Kibana version and configuration. Exporting a Discover session definition as JSON does not export the log events themselves. For LogTotal, use a supported log format. When JSONL is required, export the records using the Python or Elasticsearch API methods described below, or convert the exported data into one JSON object per line before uploading. Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Look it over before you continue. Review. Alerts live in their own indices (.alerts-security.alerts-*). Exporting alerts is a different job from exporting the logs behind them; for LogTotal, export the logs. Does this work for OpenSearch? The idea is the same, the clients differ.

Elastic is one of the most common foundations for in-house security analytics, from Elastic Security to self-built stacks. Prime Core has 23,722 detection rules for Elastic, mapped to 671 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Authentication. Create an API key in Stack Management → API keys with read and view_index_metadata on the indices you need. Send it as Authorization: ApiKey . On Elastic Cloud, the Elasticsearch endpoint is on your deployment’s overview page.

Know where the data lives. Elastic Agent integrations write to data streams named logs--. Linux authentication logs from the System integration, for example, land in logs-system.auth-default.

Check for event.original. Many integrations don’t keep the raw line by default; it’s a “preserve original event” option. If it’s missing, the parsed fields are what you have, and that’s fine for a JSON upload.

Data tiers. Searches against cold or frozen tiers are slower. Keep windows tight when the data is old.

The examples follow the current Elastic documentation, checked October 2026.

Option 1: Python with helpers.scan (recommended) 
import json, os
from elasticsearch import Elasticsearch, helpers

es = Elasticsearch("https://my-deployment.es.example.com:443", api_key=os.environ["ES_API_KEY"])
query = {"query": {"range": {"@timestamp": {
    "gte": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "lt": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"}}}}

with open("elastic_auth_1019.jsonl", "w") as out:
    for hit in helpers.scan(es, index="logs-system.auth-*", query=query, size=1000):
        out.write(json.dumps(hit["_source"]) + "\n")

For raw lines, write hit[“_source”].get(“event”, {}).get(“original”, “”) instead of the whole document.

Option 2: ES|QL for quick pulls

In Kibana Dev Tools:

POST /_query?format=json
{
  "query": """
    FROM logs-system.auth-*
    | WHERE @timestamp >= "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z" AND @timestamp < "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"
    | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, source.ip, message
    | LIMIT 10000
  """
}

Two catches. ES|QL returns 1,000 rows unless you set LIMIT, and it tops out at 10,000. The JSON response also comes as columns plus values, not as records. To turn it into one object per line, save the query body as query.json and run it through jq:

curl -sS -H "Authorization: ApiKey $ES_API_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  "https://my-deployment.es.example.com/_query?format=json" -d @query.json \
  | jq -c '.columns as $c | .values[] | [$c, .] | transpose | map({(.[0].name): .[1]}) | add' > esql_1019.jsonl
Option 3: Export logs from Kibana UI (Discover)

For smaller investigations, Kibana Discover lets you find, filter, and export logs directly from the browser without writing scripts.

  1. Open Discover. Sign in to Kibana and navigate to Analytics → Discover, or select Discover from the main navigation.
  2. Select your data. Choose the data view containing the logs you need, such as logs-system.auth-*. Make sure it includes the relevant Elasticsearch indices or data streams.
  3. Set the time range. Use the time picker in the upper-right corner to select the investigation period. Narrow the window to avoid exporting unnecessary events.
  4. Filter the logs. Use the search bar and available filters to isolate relevant events. For example, enter event.category: authentication to focus on authentication activity.
  5. Select the fields. Add useful columns such as @timestamp, host.name, user.name, source.ip, and message. If available, include event.original to preserve the raw log content.
  6. Export the results. Open More → Export → Tab results as CSV (in some versions, Share → CSV Reports). Generate the report and download the CSV file. If the export is not downloaded immediately, find it under Stack Management → Reporting.

Alternative: Copy logs as JSON. For a small selection of events, select the relevant rows in Discover, open the Selected menu, and choose Copy documents as JSON. Paste the copied content into a text editor and save it as a .json file. Only the fields included in the current table selection may be copied.

Limitations. CSV reports are intended for moderate-sized exports and have row-count and file-size limits that depend on the Kibana version and configuration. Exporting a Discover session definition as JSON does not export the log events themselves.

For LogTotal, use a supported log format. When JSONL is required, export the records using the Python or Elasticsearch API methods described below, or convert the exported data into one JSON object per line before uploading.

  2. Sanitize. Look it over before you continue.
  3. Review.

items.title: Trezor Warns of Suspected Spy Implant in Crypto Wallet That Could Steal Recovery Phrases
items.summary: Trezor has warned that a suspected hardware implant inside a Trezor Safe 5 could steal recovery phrases and send them over a mobile network. The warning covers every Trezor model bought from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onward, although only one suspected device has been reported. In its October 30 security notice , Trezor urged affected users to move funds to a newly created wallet with a new seed. The company has not examined the device and has received no reports of stolen funds from CryptoBilis buyers. The March cutoff is a precautionary scope for customer action, not proof that every device sold since then was altered. The confirmed extent and operation of the suspected Trezor implant remain subject to laboratory examination. Suspected Implant Targets the Wallet Screen The report came from a customer in Indonesia who bought the Safe 5 through CryptoBilis on Tokopedia in August 2026. Trezor received the disclosure on October 28, reviewed photos, and interviewed the customer by video. The device is being sent to its security lab.[ trezor ] According to the report, an extra circuit board sits between the wallet’s main board and screen. It contains a cellular module and antenna. The added hardware allegedly reads information shown on the display, including the wallet backup, and sends it over a mobile network while the device is plugged in. That would make the screen connection a possible theft point. Rather than needing to break the wallet’s core security, an attacker could capture the recovery words when they appear during setup. This remains a reported method, not a finding confirmed through Trezor’s own testing. A stolen recovery phrase can let someone restore a wallet elsewhere and control its funds. Cybersecurity News has also covered fake crypto wallet screens that seek the same secret through false recovery prompts. The suspected implant would target displayed information instead of relying on a user entering words into fake software. The warning follows a separate investigation involving Ledger wallets supplied by CryptoBilis. According to Trezor, Ledger began investigating customer fund losses on October 9 and later confirmed physical tampering in some devices. Cybersecurity News previously reported Ledger’s confirmation of an unauthorized hardware implant in a CryptoBilis device. Trezor removed CryptoBilis from its authorized reseller network on October 9 and began checking customer devices. Despite the shared reseller, Trezor has not identified the attackers or confirmed that the same group targeted both brands. It is working with Ledger and other parties investigating the incident. Trezor also credited SEAL 911, the Security Alliance’s emergency response service, for helping with the report and customer support planning. The customer who reported the suspected Trezor implant had already moved his funds before finding it. Trezor says it has received no reports involving other resellers. Its warning also covers stores selling devices supplied by CryptoBilis, not just purchases made directly from the reseller. What Affected Trezor Owners Should Do Trezor says moving the existing wallet backup onto another device does not fix the risk. Users need a fresh wallet with a newly generated seed, then must transfer their funds to it. Anyone who has not set up an affected device should leave it unused and never enter an existing recovery phrase. If another secure hardware wallet is unavailable, Trezor recommends temporarily using a software wallet or familiar exchange. Its sending guide explains the transfer process. Users should carefully check the full receiving address before sending funds. Customers should not rely on weighing or opening their devices to rule out tampering. Trezor says weight differences can have other causes and there is no dependable home inspection method. Eligible CryptoBilis buyers can contact official Trezor Support for a replacement shipped directly or a voucher covering a new device. They should keep the original wallet. Trezor also warns that scammers may exploit the incident through fake emails, letters, or calls. Support will never ask for a recovery phrase.

items.summary_html:
Yesterday, Anthropic were compromised and Cursor VS Code extension used by tens of millions of developers for Claude access was delivering a remote access trojan via an SSH reverse backdoor. The malware allowed hands on and automated remote access to developer laptops and desktops, in a supply chain attack.

Anthropic has not informed customers, and the malicious version was silently deleted without telling anybody.

The extension itself auto updated in Cursor to the malicious version. Cursor say around 5000 developer systems were impacted.

Phorion were the first to notice the malicious activity on endpoints:

Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory | Phorion

The compromised version was 2.1.313. This version was replaced 8 hours ago by Anthropic, with version 2.1.314, which appears to remove the backdoor from the extension but I’m not sure if it still contains no malicious code. It does not remove the SSH backdoor from systems already infected, nor the prior recon activity.

You may notice 2.1.313 is missing from OpenVSX, Visual Studio Marketplace and Cursor:

Cursor has admitted the issue:

Security notice - malicious version of Anthropic.claude-code (2.1.313) identified in the Cursor Extension Marketplace · Cursor

a maliciously modified version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was made available in the Cursor VS Code extension Marketplace. The extension runs malicious code that attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor. Specifically, it:
Collects host and user information: hostname, username, OS, architecture, home directory path, environment variable names, working directories, configured Git email, and public IP.
Attempts to add an attacker-controlled SSH key to authorized_keys, enable the local SSH service, and open a reverse SSH tunnel. Outside of highly unusual circumstances where Cursor was started with administrator privileges, due to errors in the malicious code, this step would fail.
Attempts to make the reverse SSH tunnel persistent via a LaunchAgent (macOS) or a scheduled task that attempts to run as SYSTEM with a Startup-script fallback (Windows). Background scripts retry the tunnel roughly every 60 seconds.
Reports host details and backdoor status via HTTP POST to /beacon on port 8099.

To hunt for the malicious version with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, I have published KQL queries:

ThreatHunting/AdvancedHuntingQueries/AnthropicSupplyChainAttack.kql at master · GossiTheDog/ThreatHunting

There is some wordsmithing in the Cursor blog, for example: “This malicious version of the extension was not developed by Anthropic” — it was, in fact, uploaded as Anthropic’s verified account. “Developed” is doing some heavy lifting — of course Anthropic didn’t develop the backdoor, there was a security incident leading to a supply chain attack.

Notable customers who run Claude Code and Cursor on laptops include Binance, amongst thousands of others.

This is an emerging situation, follow me on Mastodon for updates — @gossithedog@cyberplace.social:

Cyberplace

Network IoCs:

  • VSIX SHA-256 (darwin-arm64 — Mac): 432ccdee3801f99e52b8fe31f69ea9870118e96ea7ef9ecabed1479621b5ab62
  • Modified VSIX SHA-256 (win32-x64): 3de1722901165769893bef57c72594e9a54459faa23f3091b136b79966edd081
Network
  • Reverse SSH tunnel: 134[.]209[.]82[.]225 port 22
  • C2: hxxp://134[.]209[.]82[.]225:8099/beacon (HTTP POST)
  • Local beacon attempt: 127[.]0[.]0[.]1:8099/beacon (HTTP POST, loopback)
  • Public IP lookups to ifconfig[.]me / api[.]ipify[.]org — legitimate services; access alone is not an indicator

Anthropic hacked to deliver remote access trojan to Claude developer laptops worldwide was originally published in DoublePulsar on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: How to Export Event Data from CrowdStrike Falcon
items.summary: For a targeted pull, run your query in Falcon’s Advanced Event Search and export the results as JSON. For bulk raw telemetry, Falcon Data Replicator (FDR) delivers your events to an S3 bucket as gzipped JSON, one event per line. Keep in mind what you’re getting: Falcon’s own sensor telemetry (process, network, DNS, logon events), not the hosts’ original Windows or Linux logs. Falcon telemetry is some of the richest endpoint data a SOC has, and it’s often the first thing an IR partner asks for. Prime Core has 23,742 detection rules for CrowdStrike data, mapped to 674 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get it out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Access. Event search needs a Falcon role that allows it. FDR needs its own subscription, plus an API client with FDR scope; CrowdStrike gives you the bucket, queue and credentials. Retention. How far back event data goes depends on your subscription, often days to a few months. Check before you promise anyone history. Event names. Falcon telemetry is organized by event_simpleName. The ones you’ll use most: ProcessRollup2 (process start), NetworkConnectIP4, DnsRequest, UserLogon. Knowing them makes queries much faster to write. CrowdStrike’s documentation sits behind the Falcon login. This guide is based on it, plus the public FalconPy and FDR projects, checked October 2026. Option 1: Advanced Event Search Scope the query tightly, and don’t reduce it with table() before exporting, because that drops fields: #event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ComputerName=WS-042 Set the time range, run the search, then export the results as JSON or CSV. If CSV is selected, specify in ‘Fields to export’ choose ‘Select all. Option 2: Falcon Data Replicator (bulk) FDR is the route for volume. CrowdStrike writes batches of gzipped JSON files to an S3 bucket and announces each new batch on an SQS queue. For continuous collection, consume the queue (CrowdStrike publishes a sample consumer). For a one-off, list the bucket, pick the batches covering your window, and download them: export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=' ' export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=' ' aws s3 ls s3:// / / --recursive | less aws s3 cp s3:// / / / ./fdr/ --recursive Then filter to the host you care about, by its agent ID: zcat ./fdr/*.gz | jq -c 'select(.aid == " ")' > ws042_fdr.jsonl Each line is one event. FDR volume adds up fast, so filter by aid and event_simpleName before you upload. Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. items.title: How to Export Logs from Microsoft Sentinel
items.summary: Sentinel data lives in a Log Analytics workspace, so an export is a KQL query plus a way to save the results as JSON. The simplest is the Azure CLI: az monitor log-analytics query returns one JSON object per row. The portal’s export button produces a spreadsheet-style file that LogTotal doesn’t read today, so use the CLI or PowerShell for uploads. Sentinel collects from everywhere: Windows, Linux, Entra ID, Microsoft 365, firewalls, clouds. That makes it the natural place to pull an investigation slice from. Prime Core has 23,700 detection rules for Microsoft Sentinel, mapped to 674 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get the data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Permissions. Log Analytics Reader or Microsoft Sentinel Reader on the workspace is enough. The workspace ID. The CLI wants the workspace GUID, from the workspace’s overview page, not its name. Know your tables. The ones that matter most: SecurityEvent (Windows), Syslog (Linux), SigninLogs and AuditLogs (Entra ID), OfficeActivity (Microsoft 365), CommonSecurityLog (CEF from firewalls and other appliances), AzureActivity, plus any custom _CL tables. Retention tiers. Data in interactive retention can be queried directly. Data that has aged into long-term retention can’t: you need a search job or a restore first. Some table plans (Basic, Auxiliary) also limit what KQL can do. Where you write KQL. Depending on how your tenant is set up, that’s Advanced hunting in the Microsoft Defender portal or Logs in the Azure portal. The queries are the same. The commands follow Microsoft’s documentation, checked October 2026. Step 1: Write the query Keep it to events. No summarize if you want logs back. For Linux SSH activity: Syslog | where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20)) | where Computer == "web-03" | where ProcessName in ("sshd", "sshd-session") For Windows logons and account changes on a domain controller: SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20)) | where Computer startswith "DC-01" Run it in the portal first and check the row count. Step 2: Export as JSON Azure CLI: az login az monitor log-analytics query \ --workspace \ --analytics-query "Syslog | where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20)) | where Computer == 'web-03'" \ --output json > sentinel_web03_1019.json jq -c '.[]' sentinel_web03_1019.json > sentinel_web03_1019.jsonl The first run may ask to install the log-analytics extension. Say yes. PowerShell (Az module): Connect-AzAccount $kql = "SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20)) | where Computer startswith 'DC-01'" (Invoke-AzOperationalInsightsQuery -WorkspaceId ' ' -Query $kql).Results | ForEach-Object { $_ | ConvertTo-Json -Compress } | Out-File sentinel_dc01_1019.jsonl -Encoding utf8 Query results are capped in rows and size. For busy tables, split the window into hours and run the export once per slice. Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix CLI asks about an extension log-analytics isn’t installed Accept, or az extension add –name log-analytics Workspace not found Name used instead of the GUID Use the workspace ID from its overview page Fewer rows than expected Result limits Split the time window Old data returns nothing It’s in long-term retention Run a search job or restore first Forbidden Missing reader role on the workspace Ask for Log Analytics Reader FAQ Do I get raw Windows events? You get the parsed SecurityEvent rows, with the original event data in the EventData column. Not an EVTX file. For EVTX, export from the host. What about Defender XDR data in Sentinel? If you use the unified Defender portal, advanced hunting can query Defender and Sentinel tables together.

items.title: How to Export Advanced Hunting Results from Microsoft Defender XDR
items.summary: Run your query in Advanced hunting , then send the same query to Microsoft Graph’s runHuntingQuery to get the results as JSON. The portal’s export button produces a spreadsheet-style file that LogTotal doesn’t read today. Advanced hunting keeps 30 days of data, so anything older has to come from Sentinel or wherever you stream Defender data. Defender XDR holds endpoint, identity, email and cloud app telemetry in one queryable place, which makes it the first stop in most Microsoft-shop investigations. Prime Core has 17,197 detection rules for Microsoft Defender data, mapped to 659 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to pull a slice out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Permissions. For Graph, you need the ThreatHunting.Read.All permission. The signed-in user also needs a Defender role that allows advanced hunting. Limits. Queries time out after a few minutes, and results are capped. Plan to split by time or by device. The tables. DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceNetworkEvents, DeviceLogonEvents, DeviceFileEvents, DeviceRegistryEvents, DeviceEvents (a mixed bag, including ASR and AMSI events), EmailEvents, IdentityLogonEvents, and AlertInfo with AlertEvidence. The time column is Timestamp. The examples follow Microsoft’s documentation, checked October 2026. Step 1: Write the query DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20)) | where DeviceName startswith "ws-042" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256 Run it in the portal first. Device names in Defender are often FQDNs, which is why startswith works better than ==. Step 2: Export through Microsoft Graph Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "ThreatHunting.Read.All" $kql = @" DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-10-19) .. datetime(2026-10-20)) | where DeviceName startswith "ws-042" "@ $resp = Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method POST ` -Uri "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/security/runHuntingQuery" ` -Body (@{ Query = $kql } | ConvertTo-Json) -ContentType "application/json" $resp.results | ForEach-Object { $_ | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress } | Out-File ws042_proc_1019.jsonl -Encoding utf8 Each row comes back as one JSON object per line. For several days or several devices, loop over day-sized windows to stay under the limits. Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix 403 from Graph Missing ThreatHunting.Read.All consent or Defender role Grant consent; check your role Query times out or returns partial results Too much data in one query Narrow the time window or the device set Nothing older than 30 days Advanced hunting retention Use Sentinel or your streaming destination Row count stops at a round number Result cap Split the window No rows for a known device Name mismatch (short name vs FQDN) Use startswith or has FAQ Can I get the raw EVTX from a device? Yes, with Live Response in Defender for Endpoint: getfile pulls files, including exported EVTX, from a machine. Is this the same as Sentinel? No, though they overlap in the unified Defender portal. Sentinel keeps longer history.

items.title: Binance Faces Largest Crypto Heist – $6.36 Billion Reportedly Stolen by North Korean Group
items.summary: Binance reportedly lost approximately $6.36 billion in cryptocurrency on October 29, 2026, after an attacker drained wallets across ten blockchains. TRM Labs describes the incident as the largest cryptocurrency theft ever recorded, with most of the stolen funds transferred out within about 20 minutes of the attack. Its investigation attributes the operation to TraderTraitor, a North Korean-linked hacking group known for targeting cryptocurrency platforms and financial organizations to steal digital assets. According to TRM, Binance acknowledged a security incident, suspended withdrawals on several networks, and said user funds were safe. The reported loss exceeds four times the $1.5 billion Bybit theft. Earlier reporting on the Bybit multistage attack investigation explains how compromised infrastructure enabled another major cryptocurrency theft, although Binance’s initial entry point remains unknown. Binance Hit by Biggest Crypto Heist in History Researchers from TRM identified malicious sweeper contract activity that allowed the attacker to repeatedly drain a Binance Ethereum hot wallet. Their published Binance hack analysis describes harmful smart contract code rather than a named endpoint malware family. TRM attributes the operation to TraderTraitor with high confidence, citing blockchain records and intelligence gathered outside the blockchain. Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft. The operator received three small Tornado Cash withdrawals starting October 28, then deployed and tested attack code against several wallets. A final rehearsal preceded installation of the same code on a Binance hot wallet by approximately four hours, suggesting a planned operation rather than an opportunistic transfer. The first recorded theft occurred on the XRP Ledger between 20:05 and 20:09 UTC, when five Binance wallets transferred 233.46 million XRP. Solana and Optimism transfers followed. At 20:20 UTC, a Bitcoin hot wallet sent 18,270 BTC to the attacker, who immediately split the funds into smaller amounts through a peel chain. Ethereum activity exposed the attack’s central technical feature: EIP-7702 delegation. This mechanism lets a wallet authorize smart contract code to control its behavior. At 20:20 UTC, the operator submitted 50 authorizations signed by Binance’s wallet, directing it toward an attacker-controlled sweeper. Unlike previously documented TraderTraitor cloud compromise campaigns , this report does not establish how access was first obtained. Each authorization covered a consecutive nonce, the counter used to track wallet activity. Preparing multiple signatures increased the chance that one would match the wallet’s current counter when executed. One matched. Three minutes and 24 seconds later, a single sweep transferred 167,464 ETH and 63 tokens, including 1.615 billion USDT. The delegation remained active, allowing six further sweeps as fresh deposits arrived. The compromised wallet also controlled execution for another Binance smart account, enabling the removal of 823 million USDC. Meanwhile, wallets across other networks produced ordinary signed transfers. TRM therefore suspects compromised signing infrastructure, not an Ethereum-only authorization phishing incident. Binance had not published a root cause in the report. Frozen Funds, Laundering Activity, and Defensive Priorities TRM valued the stolen assets at their prices when transferred, producing the $6.36 billion estimate. Ethereum accounted for approximately $3.79 billion, followed by Bitcoin at $1.47 billion and Tron at $628 million. Its figures reflect blockchain observations through October 30 at 00:30 UTC, meaning subsequent movements or price changes could alter later assessments. Issuers and network responders restricted approximately $2.7 billion. Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial froze stablecoins, while Arbitrum’s Security Council removed 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB from the attacker’s control. These actions limited access to funds; they did not establish that the assets had been returned to Binance. The attacker also converted approximately 325 million USDT into roughly 122,300 ETH through market makers and trading contracts. Another wallet deposited 60 million USDT into Aave and borrowed about 19,760 ETH. Earlier investigations into Lazarus cryptocurrency laundering networks illustrate why tracing counterparties matters, although those findings should not be treated as proof of participants in this incident. TRM recommends screening deposits and trading counterparties, alerting on unexpected wallet delegations, and rejecting unapproved EIP-7702 authorizations. Exchanges should separate signing systems and approval paths across blockchains and wallet tiers. Treasury teams also need tested revocation procedures because a malicious delegation can keep redirecting incoming funds after the initial theft. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Indicator type Source-reported observation Wallet delegation Unexpected EIP-7702 code on treasury wallets Signing behavior Batch of 50 consecutive-nonce authorizations Fund movement Repeated sweeps of incoming deposits Bitcoin laundering Peel-chain outputs of 1,000 and 100 BTC Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: How to Export Logs from Google SecOps (Chronicle)
items.summary: For small, targeted pulls, run a UDM search and call the same search through the Google SecOps API to get JSON. For raw logs in their original format, the Data Export API copies logs for a time range and log type into a Cloud Storage bucket you own. The UI’s export produces a spreadsheet-style file that LogTotal doesn’t read today. Google SecOps keeps a year of data by default at Google scale, and it’s increasingly where security teams look first. Prime Core has 20,031 detection rules for Google SecOps, mapped to 663 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Raw logs or UDM events? Google SecOps keeps both: the raw logs as ingested, and normalized UDM events. When the raw logs are syslog or JSON, they’re usually the better input for LogTotal. UDM JSON works too. Permissions. Access is granted through IAM roles on the SecOps instance. A data export also needs permission to create exports and a bucket the SecOps service account can write to. Retention. Standard retention is 12 months. Log types. Every feed has a log type label, such as WINEVTLOG for Windows event logs. Note the ones you need before you export. The steps follow Google’s documentation, checked October 2026. Endpoints differ by region and API version, so check them against your instance. Option 1: UDM search through the API Write the search in the UI first, for example principal.hostname = “web-03”, and check the results. Then run it through the API with a time range: TOKEN=$(gcloud auth print-access-token) curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ "https:// -chronicle.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/ /locations/ /instances/ :udmSearch?query=principal.hostname%3D%22web-03%22&timeRange.startTime=2026-10-19T00:00:00Z&timeRange.endTime=2026-10-20T00:00:00Z&limit=10000" \ | jq -c '.events[]' > secops_web03_1019.jsonl Option 2: Raw logs with the Data Export API For larger windows, or when you want logs exactly as they arrived: Create a Cloud Storage bucket and give the SecOps service account write access to it. Create a data export for your time range and log type, pointing at the bucket. Poll the export until it finishes. Download the files: gcloud storage cp -r gs://my-secops-export/ / ./secops-export/ The files hold the original log lines for that log type. Decompress them if needed, then upload. Option 3: Export logs through the Google SecOps UI For quick investigations or smaller log samples, you can export search results directly from the Google SecOps interface without using the API. Set the time range and click Run Search . Review results. Check the matching events. For UDM searches, use the Column Manager to select the fields you want to export. Download the logs. UDM events: In the Events table, click Download and select Download as CSV . You can also select Download as CSV (with raw logs) to include the original log entries. Raw logs: In the Raw Logs results table, click More > Download as CSV . Save the file. Google SecOps downloads the results as a CSV file. Limitations. For larger exports, narrow the time range or use the Data Export API. To analyze the exported data in LogTotal, extract the original log entries into a supported raw log format or use the API export methods described above. Step 3: Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Review. items.title: Unauthorized OpenAI Codex and Claude Code Relays Disable AI Sandboxes and Redirect Enterprise Data
items.summary: An unauthorized AI relay service is installing genuine OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code tools on company computers, then changing their settings to send requests through third-party servers. The setup also removes sandbox controls, creating a path for sensitive business data to leave approved systems. Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team documented the activity in an October 29 report. Researchers observed the service across a dozen organizations since early 2026. Most were in mainland China, with other deployments involving multinational firms connected to South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia. Affected industries include semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, shipping, electronics, petrochemicals, and data center services. The key distinction is configuration. Researchers found neither a modified client nor a vulnerability in Codex or Claude Code. The genuine tools follow settings introduced by the relay. Sandbox Controls and Credentials Replaced Users appear to run a setup command themselves, often within minutes to half an hour of installing an AI coding tool through npm. Researchers found no automated or exploit-based delivery. A fileless PowerShell or bash script arrives from a lookalike domain such as vibe.aiok[.]me . It checks for Node.js and the requested coding tool, installs missing components, and then applies the relay settings. Because users receive a working application, the extra setup can look routine. The script rewrites ~/.codex/config.toml or ~/.claude/settings.json . It changes base_url or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to relay-controlled infrastructure and installs relay-issued credentials. User-level environment variables preserve these settings after a restart. For teams examining unfamiliar setup scripts, ANY.RUN’s interactive sandbox offers a separate analysis environment with live interaction and reporting. This differs from the coding agent’s own sandbox, which limits actions during normal use. In Codex, the script sets sandbox_mode to danger-full-access . It also enables network access for the write sandbox and disables telemetry and error reporting through DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 and DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING=1 . These changes remove safeguards while suppressing signals that might otherwise reach the vendors. On one host, the script ran claude /logout , removed ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , then ran claude /login . This cleared an existing session before relay credentials took over. Researchers could not establish whether every deployment followed that sequence, reads the Symantec report . The service rotated through at least eight domains imitating OpenAI or Anthropic services. Its subscription-style Claude tokens could suggest pooled account resale, but researchers said this was not proof of its business model. Related reporting on Codex and Claude Code hijacking through Downloads folders shows a separate route to endpoint redirection. Here, however, the setup script changes the settings directly rather than relying on malicious instructions inside files. The relay can see prompts, files, and secrets sent through it, and could alter responses. With sandbox protection removed, a malicious response could lead to commands running with the user’s account privileges. Symantec found no evidence that the operator had exploited this position. Observed redirection must not be confused with confirmed data theft. Separate coverage of AI coding agent security flaws highlights why permission controls matter. This case adds another concern: genuine software can become unsafe when an unapproved service controls its settings. Defenders should review endpoint URLs, sandbox settings, and user-level credential variables. PowerShell or bash download-and-execute commands shortly after npm installation deserve attention. Network monitoring should flag coding tools contacting destinations outside approved AI endpoints. Relay-issued variables also warrant review because other applications may inherit them. These checks help separate sanctioned deployments from unapproved access without treating every legitimate AI installation as malicious activity. items.title: CISA Warns of GitLab Integer Overflow Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks
items.summary: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has warned that attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-97229 . This GitLab vulnerability could allow code execution without logging in. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 29, 2026, confirming evidence of active exploitation and raising the urgency for organizations running affected GitLab servers. The vulnerability affects GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition. It involves an integer overflow or wraparound caused by insufficient checks on regular expressions inside CI/CD configurations. A specially crafted expression could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server. Cybersecuritynews.com previously covered the technical details in its report on the GitLab code execution vulnerability . Regular expressions are text patterns used to match or filter data. In this case, the dangerous input reaches GitLab’s regular expression compiler through a CI/CD configuration. These configurations define automated development tasks. Processing a malicious pattern could affect the server itself, not just cause a pipeline task to fail. GitLab Integer Overflow Vulnerability Exploited An integer overflow occurs when a calculation produces a number outside the range a program can store. The resulting value can become unexpectedly small or negative. MITRE’s CWE-190 description explains that these errors can cause crashes, memory corruption, or unauthorized code execution, depending on how the software uses the value. GitLab assigned the flaw a maximum CVSS score of 10.0. Earlier reporting identified affected versions as 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.4, and 19.4 before 19.4.2. Those branches received fixes on October 12. Administrators should review their installed release and follow the current vendor update guidance. The supplied catalog entry lists November 1, 2026, as the remediation deadline and marks forensic triage as required under BOD 26-04. It lists ransomware use as unknown. That status does not establish a ransomware link, and CISA’s public alert does not identify attackers, victims, or the scale of exploitation. CISA’s October 29 alert explains that BOD 26-04 requires federal civilian agencies to prioritize high-risk vulnerabilities on exposed assets. The directive also requires, where applicable, checks for signs that attackers compromised a system before updates were applied. CISA encourages other organizations to adopt similar risk-based patching practices. Administrators must also avoid confusing this issue with CVE-2026-110264, a separate GitLab regular expression vulnerability disclosed later in October. Cybersecuritynews.com’s coverage of that separate GitLab server vulnerability explains that installing the earlier CVE-2026-97229 update does not fix the newer issue. Reviewing both advisories helps teams choose an update that addresses both vulnerabilities rather than leaving another code execution path open on their GitLab servers. items.title: Ivanti Connect Secure 0-Days Exploited in the Wild to Gain Unauthenticated Root Access
items.summary: Attackers are chaining zero-day flaws in Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances to gain unauthenticated root access, exposing stored credentials and sensitive Active Directory data. Ivanti confirmed attacks against a limited number of customers and released additional fixes on October 29, 2026, following its initial October patches. Volexity tracked UTA0576 activity to October 3 and, during an October 5 investigation, identified a compromised, fully patched Ivanti appliance running version 22.8R2.4 (Build 19097) during an investigation on October 5, highlighting the flaws’ ability to bypass existing protections. According to Volexity’s technical analysis , the attack began with an authentication bypass in welcome.cgi, the public login script. A mismatch between the requested URL and the X-DSCGI-PATH header let the attacker reach a protected upload handler without signing in. The upload handler, wu.cgi, wrote incoming content to a predictable temporary location before checking whether it was a valid ZIP file. The attacker uploaded a Perl script and sent parallel requests to execute it before the appliance deleted it. This timing flaw delivered code execution as the appliance’s cgi-server user. Ivanti Memory Analysis with Volexity Volcano (source: Volexity ) The attacker then abused the privileged dsinvoked service. By changing library code in memory and altering a maintenance task in the DSCache configuration store, UTA0576 caused the service to run attacker-controlled code as root. items.title: Accenture Contractor Allegedly Gave Claude AI Agent Access to Secure Pentagon Network
items.summary: An Accenture employee allegedly gave a personal Claude Code AI agent administrative access to a secure U.S. Department of Defense environment, allowing it to write and deploy code. The agent reportedly operated for about two months and appears to have sent credentials and network details to an outside website. Accenture disputes the allegations, saying an independent investigation found them without merit. According to WIRED’s investigation , published October 29, the system serves multiple intelligence agencies and holds Controlled Unclassified Information, or CUI. This information is not classified, but still requires protection against unauthorized release. Claude AI Agent Allegedly Gained Access The employee reportedly connected a personal account for Anthropic’s Claude Code to a production environment on the nonclassified Internet Protocol Router Network, known as NIPRNet. Unlike classified military networks, NIPRNet connects to the internet while supporting protected government work. WIRED’s sources said the contractor shared login credentials so the agent could automate coding and cloud server setup. That reportedly gave it administrator rights and allowed it to bypass controls applied during normal login. Its work included writing code and committing changes under the employee’s identity. During those tasks, the agent appears to have transmitted passwords, login details, and a map of NIPRNet to a third-party website. WIRED withheld the site’s name and reported that NIST had identified a high-risk weakness that could let attackers inject instructions into an AI coding agent to steal credentials. The report does not establish that attackers exploited that weakness here. The concern overlaps with indirect prompt injection attacks , where hidden commands in outside content trick an agent into taking unauthorized actions. However, the exact cause of the alleged data transfer remains unclear. Security experts told WIRED that combining separate pieces of unclassified information can reveal details sensitive enough to warrant classification. A network map could also help an intruder locate valuable systems and understand how they connect. There is no indication that attackers accessed classified or top-secret networks. Former NSA hacker Jake Williams described another possible risk: stolen credentials could let attackers alter software developed on NIPRNet before it moves into more sensitive environments. A hidden backdoor could then travel with approved code. This was a potential attack path described by experts, not a confirmed outcome. Related reporting on AI agents exposing credentials highlights how routine tool use can reveal secrets without malware. Narrow permissions, short-lived credentials, and restricted network access can reduce that exposure. Accenture Rejects the Claims Accenture told WIRED that the allegations were “thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit.” It said it met its legal and contractual duties but did not identify the investigator. The Pentagon declined to discuss its network status. WIRED also reported claims that Accenture did not initially notify the government. Those claims remain disputed. The publication placed Accenture’s federal contracts above $3.5 billion, including nearly $605 million with the Defense Department, underscoring the stakes of oversight across its government work. items.title: CISA Warns of Linux Kernel Missing Initialization Vulnerability Exploited in Attacks
items.summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has warned that attackers are exploiting a Linux kernel vulnerability (CVE-2026-46300) that can help them gain control of affected systems. The flaw was added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 28, 2026, placing it among security issues with confirmed exploitation. CISA’s catalog entry sets an October 31 remediation deadline and requires forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. The agency says attackers can chain the kernel flaw with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to implant PHP webshells and run commands as root. It remains unknown whether the vulnerability has been used in ransomware campaigns. The flaw affects how the Linux kernel combines network data held in socket buffers. According to the official CVE record, the skb_try_coalesce() function can transfer fragments backed by shared memory or the page cache without preserving the SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG marker. This marker tells later code that the data needs special handling before modification. When that marker disappears, the kernel can incorrectly treat shared fragments as safe to change directly. During Encapsulating Security Payload, or ESP, input processing, the kernel may skip a protective copying step and decrypt data in place. This can modify page-cache-backed data that should not have been changed through that path. The published CVSS score is 7.8, rated high severity. Its assessment describes a local attack requiring low privileges and no user interaction. Linux Kernel Missing Initialization Vulnerability Exploited That is important because the kernel flaw alone should not be described as an unauthenticated remote takeover. CISA’s warning instead highlights its use alongside other vulnerabilities in a broader attack chain. The upstream fix preserves the shared-fragment marker when paged fragments move between socket buffers. The CVE record identifies fixed releases across several maintained branches, including Linux 5.10.257, 5.15.208, 6.1.174, 6.6.141, 6.12.91, 6.18.33, and 7.0.10. Linux 7.1 is also listed as unaffected. Administrators should follow their Linux distribution or product vendor’s guidance when selecting updates. CISA’s entry calls for vendor-approved mitigations, checks of internet exposure, and compliance with applicable patching and forensic requirements. When mitigations aren’t available, it instructs organizations to stop using the affected product. The warning follows earlier reports of Linux kernel vulnerabilities actively exploited and a separate Linux kernel privilege escalation vulnerability exploited in attacks . Those cases also involved short remediation deadlines and forensic review, showing why patching and checking for compromise must remain separate tasks. For affected organizations, the immediate concern is the combination of confirmed exploitation, possible root access, and a tight deadline. The CISA alert makes this an urgent security response, not a routine update. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Polymarket Hacked – Users Reported Funds Stolen From Their Wallets
items.summary: Polymarket suffered a security incident on October 29, 2026, after a compromised third-party provider exposed users of its international platform to wallet theft. Traders reported missing funds, unexpected withdrawals, and positions being closed without permission. The company temporarily stopped trading, said it had fixed the issue, and promised to reimburse affected users. Trading later resumed. In its public statement , Polymarket said an outside provider had been compromised and that the matter had been referred to law enforcement. Although early descriptions pointed to an authentication provider, current reporting connects this incident to DebugBear, a website performance monitoring service. Polymarket’s own statement did not name the vendor. Malicious Script Targeted Active Trading Sessions Hudson Rock’s technical investigation found malicious JavaScript served through a DebugBear address associated with Polymarket. Instead of simply measuring page performance, the code searched for an active trading session, checked account information, and attempted to use the platform’s existing trading tools to move assets. Researchers downloaded the file twice and received identical copies. The script read browser storage containing account details, a wallet address, and trading API credentials. It then searched the application’s React components for a live trading client and its signer, the tool used to authorize wallet actions. This approach attempted to reuse access already available inside a logged-in session rather than relying on a stolen password alone. Its behavior varied by account type. One route attempted to transfer position tokens directly, while another tried to sell positions before moving available funds. Researchers also found code requesting signatures and submitting transactions through Polymarket’s relayer. However, they did not execute the sample, so the findings show intended behavior rather than proof that every attempted transfer succeeded. According to CNBC’s reporting , analysis from Betting Intelligence and Polysights linked at least $2.7 million in withdrawals to 710 wallets. These figures remain outside estimates, not an officially confirmed loss total. CNBC also reported that Polymarket’s separate United States platform was not compromised. Polymarket said affected traders would be made whole. CNBC reported that users with less than $10,000 stolen were told their funds would be restored by October 30, while larger claims would require a release form. The reimbursement pledge addresses financial losses, but the exact exposure window and initial method used to compromise the provider remain unresolved. The incident highlights risks from outside scripts running on sensitive pages. Cybersecurity News previously covered an Adform compromise that distributed crypto-stealing code , showing how trusted infrastructure can become a delivery route. Its coverage of the compromised XRPL JavaScript package describes a separate supply-chain attack aimed at wallet keys. These cases involve different theft methods, but share dependence on outside code. Users should close potentially exposed tabs, review recent orders and wallet transactions through trusted channels, and save transaction hashes for support claims. Unexpected signing requests should be rejected. Hudson Rock also recommends reviewing sessions and permissions with official support, avoiding unsolicited recovery links, and never sharing a seed phrase. Disconnecting a wallet alone does not reverse completed transfers or remove existing blockchain approvals. Users should verify compensation instructions through official channels rather than messages from unfamiliar accounts. AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. items.title: World’s Largest Crypto Exchange Binance Hacked, Over $5.7 Billion Reportedly Stolen
items.summary: Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, has suspended deposits and withdrawals while investigating a suspected security breach involving billions of dollars in digital assets. Reports suggest that around $5.7 billion may have left wallets linked to the exchange, although Binance has not confirmed the total stolen or established that every flagged transfer belongs to the attack. If verified, the incident could become the largest cryptocurrency theft on record. Update1: Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Impact With Suspects DevOps Laptop Compromise In an official statement on X, Binance promised to cover all losses and said its teams were conducting security checks, freezing funds, and working with law enforcement. “User funds are safe,” the exchange said, adding that it would publish a full post-mortem once the investigation ends. The statement did not identify the entry point, name an attacker, or provide a reopening date. We are working non-stop to resolve this issue. Binance will cover all losses. As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds, and works with law enforcement. We are working around the clock and will… pic.twitter.com/zufWJ6V05D — Binance (@binance) October 30, 2026 Suspicious Transfers Span Multiple Blockchains Early reports linked the suspected Binance hack to large transfers across Ethereum, Bitcoin, and TRON. Reported outflows included approximately $1.45 billion in Bitcoin and $875 million in Ether, alongside stablecoins and other tokens. However, estimates changed as investigators examined additional wallets. Axios reported that analysts and traders placed the suspected theft between $1.7 billion and $5.7 billion, showing how uncertain the initial figures remain. That distinction matters because a wallet transfer does not, by itself, prove theft. Investigators still need to separate attacker-controlled movements from exchange activity and establish which receiving addresses belong to the same operation. Some wider estimates include Bitcoin and TRON outflows that had not yet been tied to the attacker. Treating the full reported outflow as a confirmed loss would therefore overstate the available evidence. Stablecoin issuers moved quickly to restrict funds connected to the suspected incident. According to Reuters , Tether froze nearly $1.57 billion, while Circle froze more than $800 million. Together, those actions blocked approximately $2.38 billion in stablecoins. Binance co-founder Yi He also said Ripple had frozen roughly $200 million. These figures describe frozen assets, not the total amount stolen or money already returned. Binance separately reported verified frozen assets of $2.54 billion, with tracing still underway. Freezing limits further movement, but it does not automatically restore funds to the exchange. Recovery remains a separate process. The response highlights why rapid communication between exchanges, token issuers, and investigators can reduce the damage after suspicious transfers are detected. Binance has not disclosed whether the suspected breach involved stolen signing keys, a compromised employee account, malicious software, or a weakness in its wallet systems. No public technical findings currently establish an attack path or identify a threat actor. Assigning blame before that evidence emerges would be premature. Previous exchange breaches show why the missing technical details matter. Cybersecurity News’ analysis of the Bybit attack described how attackers compromised a wallet provider’s environment and changed transaction data during a legitimate transfer. That case provides context, but it does not establish a connection to Binance or prove that the same method was used here. Binance’s promise to cover all losses is significant, but its final cost remains unknown. Reporting places its Secure Asset Fund for Users, known as SAFU, at roughly $1 billion in Bitcoin. A substantially larger confirmed shortfall could require resources beyond that emergency reserve. No detailed compensation plan has been published. The investigation also faces a familiar recovery challenge. Cybersecurity News’ report on tracing stolen Bybit funds explains how investigators combined private communications with blockchain records to identify laundering activity. For Binance, the next essential disclosures are a verified loss figure, affected wallet details, the root cause, and a safe reopening timeline. Until then, users should follow the exchange’s official updates rather than treat circulating estimates as settled facts. Update: Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Impact, Suspects DevOps Laptop Compromise Binance has raised the estimated impact of its security incident to $6.3 billion, with around $3 billion in affected assets frozen on-chain through blockchain partners. In its latest official statement , the exchange said its initial investigation suggests a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop may have allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it has found no evidence of a wallet private key leak, but stressed that the investigation remains ongoing. This is a developing story; we will keep on posted on we have updates.

In its latest official statement, the exchange said its initial investigation suggests a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop may have allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

Binance said it has found no evidence of a wallet private key leak, but stressed that the investigation remains ongoing.

This is a developing story; we will keep on posted on we have updates.

items.summary: KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 in Salt Lake City will bring the cloud native community together with projects, vendors and end users in what is one of the largest open source events. In this post, we highlight content specifically targeted at end users and session recommendations from members of the CNCF End User Technical Advisory Board (TAB) , along with practical tips for making the most of the event. Birds of Feather (BoF) Newly introduced at Kubecon EU in Amsterdam back in March, we will again have a series of BoF sessions in Salt Lake City. Last time we had packed rooms discussing and brainstorming around AI infrastructure and platforms, AI observability and optimized infrastructure for training, inference and GPU efficiency. This time around we’ll open the floor to our newly formed end user groups , the TAB recently approved end user groups covering Platform Engineering, Public Sector, Telecom and Research. And in another session we will give ourselves a challenge: get end users in one room and try to build live a reference architecture for Agentic AI deployments. It’s not clear how far we will get given how fast things are moving and how different use cases can be… but it should be a good learning session and it will definitely be fun! Town Hall In Amsterdam we chose to move the End User TAB Town Hall to the project pavilion and that was well received. So we’re keeping it this way and you can come and ask us questions right next to where the projects are located. Poster sessions Did you know Kubecon has a poster session ? It’s an ideal setting to have more in-depth discussions with the authors and there are several end user focused presentations this time around. And as always, see below for recommendations on interesting content for end users from the members of the TAB. Joseph Sandoval Surviving the Churn: Read Replicas and Controllers for Busy Kubernetes Clusters (Nov 10, 12:20 PM, Salt Palace, Grand Ballroom ACE). Your apiserver is one ordered log with everyone yelling at it, and when watchers fall behind, they get 410 Gone and relist, which makes it worse. Anthropic’s war story: one innocent LIST sent a cluster of tens of thousands of nodes into a doom spiral, twice in two weeks. Some of us have the scars. N Clusters, One kubectl: Multi-Cluster That Just Works (Nov 10, 3:40 PM, Hyatt Regency, Salt Lake Ballroom C). OCM-style multi-cluster fixes the fleet problem and creates a developer problem: the hub template is the source of truth, so the kubectl scale you just ran quietly gets reverted. Salesforce and NVIDIA built a proxy that makes the fleet feel like one cluster again, kubectl edit included. Every platform fix sends a bill to somebody else, and this talk shows what it took to pay that one down. Anatomy of an Outage: When Bursty ML Workloads Break the Kubernetes Scheduler (Nov 11, 11:00 AM, Salt Palace, Grand Ballroom H). Pending workloads timed out webhooks and took down a control plane, which probably looked fine in the design review. Isomorphic Labs and Google walk through how they stabilized it with decoupled queues and Kueue tuning. I’m looking forward to reviewing the receipts. Hardening Kubernetes for GovCloud: A 3-Year Journey to FedRAMP Moderate Authorization (Nov 11, 11:50 AM, Salt Palace, Grand Ballroom ACE). Three years to an ATO sounds about right to anyone who has argued with an auditor over a deploy pipeline. Kudos to the Verkada team for building their own deployment system to meet the isolation rules, then taking on FedRAMP’s patching mandates. If you work in a regulated environment or are working on it, be front and center for the lessons learned. Juliano Martinez Zero Downtime CNI Migration at Scale: Canal to Cilium Across Hundreds of Production Clusters (Nov 10, 4:40 PM, Salt Palace, Level 1, 151). Migrating a CNI plugin in production is one of the most high-risk operations in Kubernetes infra. At Walmart running hundreds of clusters across cloud and on-premises environments, the team faced route-drop failures in Flannel beyond 300 nodes, iptables rule explosion as services grew and etcd v2 incompatibility blocking upgrades. No published playbook existed for zero-downtime CNI replacement at that scale. Saturated by Design – Maximizing Cluster Allocation in On-Premises Kubernetes (Nov 10, 11:30 AM). On-premises compute is inelastic, and the costs are mostly up-front. Yet workload demands and hardware health can change at any time. How do you make the most of your on-premises investments without risking capacity overruns and potential outages? Running Secure Agents at Scale (Nov 11, 5:00 PM, Salt Palace, Level 1, Grand Ballroom GI). Building secure and scalable agents at scale is hard. From multi-tenancy and noisy-neighbor risk to tool access and data boundaries, teams need more than a prompt and a container image; they need a deliberate execution model. From Packets to Paychecks: eBPF-Based Network Cost Attribution at Scale (Nov 12, 11:50 AM, Salt Palace, Level 1, Grand Ballroom BDF). Cloud provider bills show egress costs as a single line item-they don’t say which tenant caused them. At Adobe, we answer that across 400K pods in 31K namespaces spanning 85+ multi-tenant Kubernetes clusters using Retina eBPF agents to capture pod-level flows at the kernel. Prometheus enriches them with node topology, and a CIDR-based classifier maps each destination IP to a cost category (Local, Internet, Peering, Transit Gateway, VPC Endpoint) with cross-AZ and cross-region modifiers that align to cloud provider billing. Kenta Tada Lessons Learned Sandboxing Agents with kagent AI agents may look like ordinary Kubernetes workloads, but their long-lived, stateful, and highly privileged behavior makes sandboxing a fundamentally different challenge. This session shares lessons from building agent sandboxing with kagent, covering filesystem and tool access, credentials, networking, identity, and cleanup, along with how NVIDIA’s OpenShell, Kubernetes’ agent-sandbox, and Google’s substrate support shape the design. GPU Observability with eBPF: From Kernel Hooks to Kubernetes Metrics GPUs are becoming a critical resource in Kubernetes, yet understanding what is happening on them remains a black box. This session shows how to build production-grade GPU observability with eBPF, from hooking into GPU interfaces and enriching telemetry with Kubernetes context to packaging programs as OCI images and integrating metrics with Prometheus and OpenTelemetry. Chad Beaudin – Boeing Birds of a Feather: Public Sector user Group The Public Sector user group recently went through the new process to be recognized as an official CNCF user group. They have been a healthy user group for a few years and I’m excited to sit in on their BoF session and hear the latest challenges (and solutions!) that leaders in that industry face. Hallway Track It’s cliche for a reason. I get so much value from talking to fellow practitioners at Kubecon. This is where I get to really find out what their pain points are, what worked for them, what their recommendations are for MY problems. Project Pavillion I love hitting the project pavilion to talk to the newer projects in the sandbox and incubation tiers. KubeCon is the one place I can talk directly to maintainers about where their project is headed, what adoption looks like in the wild, and where the technical gaps are. Ricardo Rocha Why We Bet the Data Platform on Kubernetes – And How AI Is Changing How We Operate It A talk for end users… by end users. Day 2 operations is one area where automation and AI start having a very significant impact. Whether you already integrated agents in your ops stack, have them reporting and recommending actions, or are thinking about it, come and listen how others are doing it Anatomy of an Outage: When Bursty ML Workloads Break the Kubernetes Scheduler An advanced topic but if you’re running ML training workloads on Kubernetes, this talk is something you should pay attention to. From end users and the people building the tools, there will be something for everyone Beyond the Cluster Boundary: Sharing GPUs at Scale Not a new topic but something we all struggle with when dealing with GPUs. In this case an integration of the virtual kubelet with Kueue, that is close to the solutions we’ve tried back where I work. Quota Isn’t Enough: Topology Aware Scheduling on Modern GPU Clusters Not all of us have a GB200 or GB300 lying around, but even if not the age of the GPU is here to bring back all the topology aware scheduling needs that take us back to the mainframe era. Looking forward to this one.
